status: Long-baseline experiments constrain the CP-violating phase and show preferences for its value, but establishing CP violation requires greater exposure and improved systematic control, per de Gouvêa et al., 2022, *Theory of Neutrino Physics—Snowmass TF11/NF08 Topical Group Report*, arXiv:2209.07983.
solved_when: A nonzero CP-violating effect in neutrino oscillations is established at a stated statistical significance, with the associated phase determined, and the result demonstrated to be robust against matter-effect and interaction-model systematics.
why: It would reveal a second, leptonic source of CP violation, providing a testable ingredient for explaining the matter–antimatter asymmetry of the universe.
key_works: de Gouvêa et al., 2022, *Theory of Neutrino Physics—Snowmass TF11/NF08 Topical Group Report*, arXiv:2209.07983.

title: Nonlinear saturation of fast neutrino flavor conversion
open: What flavor state do fast neutrino flavor instabilities actually settle into within realistic, collisional, inhomogeneous supernova and merger environments, and how should that outcome be coupled to the fluid evolution?
status: Linear-instability criteria are much better understood than nonlinear outcomes. A 2026 study (Akaho et al., 2026, *Bifurcated Impact of Neutrino Fast Flavor Conversion on Core…*, DOI: 10.1103/fksy-1jtw) found progenitor-dependent effects, showing that simplified universal prescriptions are insufficient.
solved_when: The final flavor distributions produced by fast instabilities are determined for realistic, collisional, inhomogeneous supernova and merger environments, and a consistent coupling to fluid evolution is achieved.
why: The nonlinear outcome alters explosion dynamics, neutrino signals, and element production.
key_works: Akaho et al., 2026, *Bifurcated Impact of Neutrino Fast Flavor Conversion on Core…* (full title verify), DOI: 10.1103/fksy-1jtw.

title: Precision neutrino–nucleus interaction model
open: Can neutrino interactions on detector nuclei be predicted and validated, across the relevant energies, to the accuracy that oscillation measurements require? The goal is a model that incorporates multinucleon effects and final-state transport and survives confrontation with data.
status: Electron scattering data, near detectors, and improved nuclear calculations constrain pieces of the problem, but model discrepancies remain an important systematic. Key work: Alvarez-Ruso et al., 2018, *NuSTEC White Paper: Status and Challenges of Neutrino–Nucleus Scattering*, arXiv:1706.03621.
solved_when: Neutrino–nucleus interaction predictions, including multinucleon effects and final-state transport, are validated across relevant energies with accuracy sufficient that interaction modeling no longer limits oscillation inference.
why: Without such a model, interaction modeling remains a limiting systematic for neutrino oscillation discoveries; with it, oscillation measurements are constrained by statistics rather than nuclear physics.
key_works: Alvarez-Ruso et al., 2018, *NuSTEC White Paper: Status and Challenges of Neutrino–Nucleus Scattering*, arXiv:1706.03621.

title: Proton spin decomposition
open: How does the proton's spin-½ arise from the spins and orbital motion of its quarks and gluons? The problem is to quantify the quark spin, gluon spin, and orbital angular momentum contributions to the proton's total angular momentum using consistent, gauge-invariant operator definitions and with controlled extrapolation to small momentum fraction.
status: The "spin crisis" dates to the late 1980s. Polarized scattering and lattice calculations determine substantial contributions, but the complete decomposition remains incomplete. Key works include Xiangdong Ji, 1997, *Gauge-Invariant Decomposition of Nucleon Spin*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.610; and Aidala et al., 2013, *The Spin Structure of the Nucleon*, arXiv:1209.2803.
solved_when: A decomposition of the proton spin into quark spin, gluon spin, and orbital contributions is available with consistent operator definitions and a controlled small-momentum-fraction extrapolation, each component determined quantitatively and summing to the total angular momentum.
why: A solution explains how a composite relativistic particle acquires its spin, resolving the long-standing "spin crisis" in hadron structure.
key_works: Xiangdong Ji, 1997, *Gauge-Invariant Decomposition of Nucleon Spin*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.610; Aidala et al., 2013, *The Spin Structure of the Nucleon*, arXiv:1209.2803.

title: Microscopic origin of the EMC effect
open: Why do nucleons bound in nuclei have different quark-gluon structure than free ones — what microscopic nuclear dynamics produces the observed modification of nuclear parton distributions, and how do short-range correlations, binding, and medium modification each contribute?
status: The effect was discovered in 1983. Strong correlations with short-range nucleon pairs are established, but their interpretation and quantitative universality remain active questions. Key works include Hen et al., 2017, *Nucleon–Nucleon Correlations, Short-Lived Excitations, and the Quarks Within*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.045002; and Kim et al., 2025, *Electromagnetic Form Factors for Nucleons in Short-Range Correlations and the EMC Effect*, DOI: 10.1103/xfkg-3m6q.
solved_when: A derivation from microscopic nuclear dynamics reproduces the observed modification of nuclear parton distributions while cleanly separating the quantitative roles of short-range correlations, binding, and medium modification.
why: It would connect quark structure with nuclear many-body physics, explaining how quark-level properties emerge inside correlated nuclear environments.
key_works: Hen et al., 2017, *Nucleon–Nucleon Correlations, Short-Lived Excitations, and the Quarks Within*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.045002; Kim et al., 2025, *Electromagnetic Form Factors for Nucleons in Short-Range Correlations and the EMC Effect*, DOI: 10.1103/xfkg-3m6q.

title: Internal structure of exotic hadrons
open: Which observed exotic resonances are genuine compact multiquark states, hadronic molecules, threshold effects, or mixtures of these — and how can we tell from data? Concretely, can pole positions of the S-matrix, combined with information from multiple production and decay channels, distinguish these binding mechanisms?
status: Many exotic candidates are established experimentally, but the discovery of a peak does not uniquely establish its binding mechanism. Key work: Brambilla et al., 2020, *The XYZ States: Experimental and Theoretical Status and Perspectives*, arXiv:1907.07583.
solved_when: A framework using pole positions and multiple production and decay channels assigns each observed exotic resonance candidate to compact multiquark, molecular, threshold-effect, or mixed categories in a way consistent across channels.
why: It maps the actual organizing principles of QCD bound states — the classification determines how the strong interaction builds matter beyond ordinary mesons and baryons.
key_works: Brambilla et al., 2020, *The XYZ States: Experimental and Theoretical Status and Perspectives*, arXiv:1907.07583.

title: Transport coefficients of the quark–gluon plasma
open: Can we compute the transport coefficients of the quark–gluon plasma — viscosities, diffusion coefficients, and related transport properties, as functions of temperature and density — directly from first principles? Formally, this requires extracting real-time transport properties from QCD with a controlled analytic continuation and quantified uncertainties.
status: Hydrodynamic fits currently constrain effective values of the coefficients, but Euclidean lattice data do not straightforwardly determine real-time spectral functions. Harvey Meyer, 2011, *Transport Properties of the Quark–Gluon Plasma: A Lattice QCD Perspective*, arXiv:1104.3708.
solved_when: Temperature- and density-dependent viscosities, diffusion coefficients, and other transport coefficients are determined from first principles, with a reliable analytic continuation from Euclidean data and explicit uncertainty estimates.
why: It converts heavy-ion collision observations into quantitative measurements of hot QCD matter; without it, such data cannot be interpreted as fundamental properties of the plasma.
key_works: Harvey Meyer, 2011, *Transport Properties of the Quark–Gluon Plasma: A Lattice QCD Perspective*, arXiv:1104.3708.

title: Predictive nuclear saturation from microscopic interactions
open: Can microscopic nuclear interactions, derived systematically from the underlying forces, predict binding energies, radii, and the saturation of nuclear matter across entire isotopic chains — with quantified, consistent uncertainties — rather than fitting each nucleus separately?
status: Chiral effective field theory and ab initio methods have advanced far beyond light nuclei, but simultaneously accurate binding and radii across broad regions of the chart remain demanding. Key works: Epelbaum, Hammer, and Meißner, 2009, *Modern Theory of Nuclear Forces*, arXiv:0811.1338; Hammer, König, and van Kolck, 2020, *Nuclear Effective Field Theory: Status and Perspectives*, arXiv:1906.12122.
solved_when: A systematically improvable interaction (e.g., from chiral effective field theory) used in ab initio calculations reproduces binding, radii, and saturation across broad isotopic chains, with uncertainty estimates propagated consistently through the many-body approximation and interaction itself.
why: It connects nuclear properties to the underlying forces rather than nucleus-by-nucleus fitting, making predictions testable where data does not exist.
key_works: Epelbaum, Hammer, and Meißner, 2009, *Modern Theory of Nuclear Forces*, arXiv:0811.1338; Hammer, König, and van Kolck, 2020, *Nuclear Effective Field Theory: Status and Perspectives*, arXiv:1906.12122.

title: Neutron lifetime reconciliation
open: Can the long-standing gap between beam and storage measurements of the neutron lifetime be closed — either by independent experiments of both kinds yielding compatible results, or by pinpointing a reproducible physical or instrumental cause of the disagreement?
status: The discrepancy has persisted for years. Proposed exotic explanations and revised corrections have been offered, but none amounts to a cross-method experimental resolution. Key works include ORPL, 2022, *Physicists Confront the Neutron Lifetime Puzzle* — as the record gives it — and Koch, 2024, *Exciting Hint toward the Solution of the Neutron Lifetime Puzzle*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.110.073004.
solved_when: Independent beam and storage experiments produce mutually compatible lifetime values, or a specific physical or instrumental source of the discrepancy is identified and demonstrated reproducibly across experiments.
why: A resolution sharpens tests of the weak interaction and tightens predictions of primordial nucleosynthesis, both of which depend directly on the neutron lifetime.
key_works: ORNL, 2022, *Physicists Confront the Neutron Lifetime Puzzle*; Koch, 2024, *Exciting Hint toward the Solution of the Neutron Lifetime Puzzle*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.110.073004.

title: Unmeasured r-process reaction rates
open: Can we determine the neutron-capture, beta-decay, and fission properties of the short-lived neutron-rich nuclei that dominate uncertainties in rapid-neutron-capture (r-process) abundance calculations? Formally, this asks for measured (or reliably constrained) nuclear data across the key region of neutron-rich species, where direct access is currently impossible.
status: Many of the relevant nuclei are inaccessible to direct conventional measurements, and theory and indirect techniques supply only incomplete substitutes.
solved_when: The neutron-capture rates, beta-decay properties, and fission properties of the short-lived neutron-rich nuclei that dominate r-process abundance uncertainties are determined at the level needed for abundance calculations.
why: It would make observed astronomical element abundances interpretable as physical histories of the events that produced them.
key_works: Cowan et al., 2021, *Origin of the Heaviest Elements: The Rapid Neutron-Capture Process*, arXiv:1901.01410; DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.93.015002.

title: Location and longevity of superheavy stability islands
open: Which proton–neutron combinations in the superheavy region are genuinely stabilized by shell effects, how do such nuclei decay, and can they actually be produced in experiments? A sharpened form asks to identify the location and half-life scale of the enhanced-stability islands and exhibit a production pathway within reach of current facilities.
status: Superheavy nuclei demonstrate shell stabilization, but the most neutron-rich predicted islands remain difficult to access; see Oganessian and Utyonkov, 2015, *Super-heavy Element Research*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/78/3/036301.
solved_when: The superheavy nuclei with enhanced stability are identified (their proton and neutron numbers located), their dominant decay channels are characterized, and an experimentally realizable production path to them is demonstrated.
why: A solution tests nuclear shell structure and relativistic quantum effects at the extreme of the nuclear chart, where conventional extrapolations of both are pushed to their limits.
key_works: Oganessian and Utyonkov, 2015, *Super-heavy Element Research*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/78/3/036301.

title: Maximum nonrotating neutron-star mass
open: What is the heaviest a cold, nonrotating neutron star can be, without assuming an overly restrictive equation-of-state parameterization? More precisely, can the maximum gravitational mass be determined in a way that does not depend on restrictive EOS modeling?
status: Heavy pulsars establish lower bounds on the maximum mass; merger remnants and population modeling provide conditional upper constraints. Key works: Lattimer and Prakash, 2016, arXiv:1512.07820; Margalit and Metzger, 2017, *Constraining the Maximum Mass of Neutron Stars from Multi-Messenger Observations of GW170817*, arXiv:1710.05938.
solved_when: A determination of the maximum gravitational mass of a cold, nonrotating neutron star is achieved that is independent of overly restrictive equation-of-state parameterizations, with its quantitative bound stated.
why: It defines the boundary between neutron stars and black holes and constrains the outcomes of neutron-star mergers.
key_works: Lattimer and Prakash, 2016, arXiv:1512.07820; Margalit and Metzger, 2017, *Constraining the Maximum Mass of Neutron Stars from Multi-Messenger Observations of GW170817*, arXiv:1710.05938.

title: Type Ia supernova progenitor fractions
open: Which physical channels actually produce Type Ia supernovae, and in what proportions? That is, determine the relative contributions of the competing white-dwarf progenitor and ignition channels across environments and over cosmic time.
status: Multiple channels can explain subsets of observations, but no single channel has been established as accounting for the full population. A key reference is Maoz, Mannucci, and Nelemans, 2014, *Observational Clues to the Progenitors of Type Ia Supernovae*, arXiv:1312.0628.
solved_when: The relative contribution of each progenitor and ignition channel is quantified across environments and cosmic time, with no single channel required to explain the full population.
why: A resolved decomposition of the progenitor channels sharpens stellar-evolution theory and grounds the physical interpretation of Type Ia supernovae as standardizable candles used in cosmology.
key_works: Maoz, Mannucci, and Nelemans, 2014, *Observational Clues to the Progenitors of Type Ia Supernovae*, arXiv:1312.0628.

title: Early supermassive-black-hole seeds
open: How did the first black holes in the Universe form and manage to grow so rapidly that they can account for the high-redshift quasar and supermassive-black-hole populations we observe? More precisely, which formation channel — stellar remnant seeds, direct collapse, or some other route — actually operated at early cosmic times, and with what characteristic seed masses and growth histories?
status: Candidate pathways exist, but seed masses, accretion duty cycles, and environmental requirements are not uniquely constrained. Key works include Volonteri, 2010, *Formation of Supermassive Black Holes*, arXiv:1003.4404, and Inayoshi, Visbal, and Haiman, 2020, *The Assembly of the First Massive Black Holes*, arXiv:1911.05791.
solved_when: The seed-formation pathways for early black holes are uniquely constrained, meaning the observed high-redshift populations can be explained by a determinate combination of channels with pinned-down seed masses, accretion duty cycles, and environmental requirements, rather than by degenerate candidate scenarios.
why: A resolution explains the early coevolution of galaxies and their central black holes, determining which growth channels can actually reproduce the observed high-redshift population.
key_works: Volonteri, 2010, *Formation of Supermassive Black Holes*, arXiv:1003.4404; Inayoshi, Visbal, and Haiman, 2020, *The Assembly of the First Massive Black Holes*, arXiv:1911.05791.

title: Species-resolved solar-wind heating
open: How do turbulent and reconnecting fields in the solar wind partition their dissipated energy among electrons, protons, and heavier ions as the wind accelerates? Formally, this asks for a species-resolved heating closure that predicts the energy split throughout solar-wind acceleration.
status: Spacecraft observations reveal anisotropic and species-dependent particle distributions, but no universal, quantitatively validated heating closure is currently available. Key works: Marsch, 2006, *Kinetic Physics of the Solar Corona and Solar Wind*; Cranmer, 2009, *Coronal Holes*. Related mathematics includes closure of weakly collisional kinetic equations.
solved_when: A universal, quantitatively validated heating closure exists that predicts how energy is partitioned among electrons, protons, and heavier ions throughout the solar-wind acceleration region, matching observed species-dependent and anisotropic distributions.
why: It connects measurable plasma kinetics to global stellar outflows, explaining spacecraft-observed species-dependent behavior from first principles.
key_works: Marsch, 2006, *Kinetic Physics of the Solar Corona and Solar Wind*; Cranmer, 2009, *Coronal Holes*.

title: Predictive solar-cycle dynamo
open: Can a physically constrained dynamo model predict the solar cycle ahead of time, determining cycle amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry, polarity reversals, and the onset of grand minima from the underlying physics rather than from empirical precursor relations?
status: Dynamo theories reproduce cyclic behavior and selected observations, but turbulent transport and the Sun's interior magnetic structure remain uncertain. Key work: Paul Charbonneau, 2020, *Dynamo Models of the Solar Cycle*, Living Reviews in Solar Physics.
solved_when: A physically constrained dynamo model demonstrably predicts these features of the solar cycle — amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry, reversals, and grand minima — ahead of time, supplanting primarily empirical precursor relations as the basis of prediction.
why: It would place long-term space-weather forecasting on a physically grounded footing rather than on statistical extrapolation.
key_works: Paul Charbonneau, 2020, *Dynamo Models of the Solar Cycle*, Living Reviews in Solar Physics.

title: Origin of the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux
open: Which populations of astrophysical sources, and what physical production environments, generate the full diffuse high-energy neutrino spectrum rather than merely individual associated events?
status: Particular sources and source classes have supporting evidence, but their integrated contribution to the diffuse flux, and the possible role of hidden-source populations, remain uncertain. Key work: Ahlers and Halzen, 2018, *Opening a New Window onto the Universe with IceCube*, arXiv:1805.11112.
solved_when: The observed diffuse neutrino flux is attributed to identified source populations and production environments whose integrated emission reproduces the full spectrum, accounting for any hidden-source contribution.
why: A solution exposes hadronic energy release that electromagnetic observations alone cannot see, since such emission may be obscured.
key_works: Ahlers and Halzen, 2018, *Opening a New Window onto the Universe with IceCube*, arXiv:1805.11112.

title: Scalable quantum repeater network
open: Can a multi-node quantum repeater network be built that delivers useful end-to-end entanglement at rates exceeding what direct transmission allows, while accounting for memory errors, channel losses, synchronization, and operational duty cycle?
status: Individual components and short network demonstrations exist; scalable integration remains the bottleneck. See Azuma et al., 2023, *Quantum Repeaters: From Quantum Networks to the Quantum Internet*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.045006.
solved_when: A demonstrated multi-node repeater network achieves end-to-end entanglement rates beyond direct-transmission limits under realistic operating conditions including memory errors, losses, synchronization, and duty cycle.
why: It enables long-distance distributed quantum systems, the foundation of a future quantum internet.
key_works: Azuma et al., 2023, *Quantum Repeaters: From Quantum Networks to the Quantum Internet*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.045006.

title: Certification of classically intractable quantum simulations
open: How can we verify that a scientifically useful quantum-simulation output is correct when exact classical checking is intractable, using affordable measurements and explicit, stated assumptions about the device?
status: Cross-checks, randomized protocols, and restricted verification schemes exist, but no universal inexpensive method certifies all practically interesting outputs. Key reference: Eisert et al., 2020, *Quantum Certification and Benchmarking*, arXiv:1910.06343.
solved_when: A certification method exists that verifies practically interesting quantum-simulation outputs at measurement cost low enough to be affordable on real devices, under explicitly formulated device assumptions, without requiring the verifier to classically simulate the computation.
why: It separates reliable scientific quantum computation from demonstrations whose outputs cannot be checked, making quantum simulation trustworthy as a scientific tool.
key_works: Eisert et al., 2020, *Quantum Certification and Benchmarking*, arXiv:1910.06343.

title: Experimental discrimination of objective-collapse models
open: Can we experimentally distinguish genuine objective collapse of the wave function from ordinary environmental decoherence? Concretely, this requires testing well-specified collapse-model parameter regions while separating predicted heating or decoherence effects from environmental noise.
status: Interferometry, mechanical sensors, and radiation bounds currently constrain collapse models; however, neither ordinary decoherence nor an unexplained excess signal alone establishes collapse. Key reference: Bassi et al., 2013, *Models of Wave-Function Collapse, Underlying Theories, and Experimental Tests*, arXiv:1204.4325.
solved_when: An experiment probes and constrains a well-defined region of collapse-model parameter space, with the predicted heating or decoherence signal cleanly separated from environmental noise sources.
why: A decisive test would tell us whether quantum mechanics itself must be modified as systems grow in mass or complexity, rather than decoherence merely masking quantum behavior.
key_works: Bassi et al., 2013, *Models of Wave-Function Collapse, Underlying Theories, and Experimental Tests*, arXiv:1204.4325.

title: Spacetime variation of fundamental constants
subfield: Atomic, molecular, and precision measurement physics
open: Do the dimensionless fundamental constants vary across space or time? A definitive answer requires detecting — or robustly constraining — correlated temporal or spatial changes in these constants using multiple clock species with independent systematic controls.
status: Clock comparisons currently give stringent null results; different transitions probe different combinations of constants. Key works: Uzan, 2011, *Varying Constants, Gravitation and Cosmology*, arXiv:1009.5514; Ludlow et al., 2015, *Optical Atomic Clocks*, arXiv:1407.3493.
solved_when: A measurement (or set of measurements) comparing multiple clock species, with systematic effects controlled independently, either detects a statistically significant correlated drift in dimensionless constants or places a robust, quantitative bound on any such temporal or spatial variation.
why: Such measurements test whether new scalar fields couple to matter and whether local position invariance — a cornerstone of general relativity — actually holds.
key_works: Uzan, 2011, *Varying Constants, Gravitation and Cosmology*, arXiv:1009.5514; Ludlow et al., 2015, *Optical Atomic Clocks*, arXiv:1407.3493.

title: Quantum-degenerate complex polyatomic molecules
subfield: Atomic, molecular, and precision measurement physics
open: Can a gas of a chosen complex polyatomic molecule be brought to quantum degeneracy while preserving low inelastic loss and controllable internal quantum states?
status: Laser cooling of polyatomic species has advanced substantially (e.g., Tarbutt, 2019, *Laser Cooling of Molecules*, arXiv:1902.05628; Augenbraun et al., 2023, *Direct Laser Cooling of Polyatomic Molecules*), but degeneracy and stable many-body control remain species-dependent frontier goals.
solved_when: A controllable quantum-degenerate gas of a specified complex polyatomic molecule is demonstrated experimentally, with low inelastic loss retained and useful internal-state control maintained.
why: It would add the rich internal structure of complex polyatomics to quantum simulation and precision tests.
key_works: Tarbutt, 2019, *Laser Cooling of Molecules*, arXiv:1902.05628; Augenbraun et al., 2023, *Direct Laser Cooling of Polyatomic Molecules*.

title: Strongly correlated dipolar molecular phases
subfield: Atomic, molecular, and precision measurement physics
open: Can specified many-body phases of polar molecules — phases driven by long-range dipolar interactions — be realized and characterized in the laboratory? Formally, the goal is regimes where long-range interactions dominate over temperature, disorder, and loss.
status: Degenerate molecular gases and controlled dipolar interactions are established ingredients; however, many predicted equilibrium and dynamical phases remain unrealized. Key works include Bohn, Rey, and Ye, 2017, *Cold Molecules: Progress in Quantum Engineering of Chemistry and Quantum Matter*; Schreck and van Druten, 2021, *Laser Cooling for Quantum Gases*.
solved_when: The targeted phases are experimentally realized and characterized, with interactions demonstrably dominating over temperature, disorder, and loss.
why: Dipolar molecular gases provide tunable models of interacting quantum matter, allowing predicted equilibrium and dynamical phases to be tested and explored.
key_works: Bohn, Rey, and Ye, 2017, *Cold Molecules: Progress in Quantum Engineering of Chemistry and Quantum Matter*; Schreck and van Druten, 2021, *Laser Cooling for Quantum Gases*.

title: Microscopic mechanism of cuprate superconductivity
open: Can a single quantitatively credible microscopic model explain cuprate high-temperature superconductivity as it is actually observed? In particular, can it derive the pairing symmetry, the transition scales, and the major normal-state trends without separately fitting each phenomenon?
status: Open since the 1986 discovery. Strong evidence constrains the pairing symmetry and important correlations, but competing mechanisms remain. Key work: Keimer et al., 2014/2015, *High Temperature Superconductivity in the Cuprates*, arXiv:1409.4673.
solved_when: A microscopic model reproduces the observed pairing, the transition scales, and the major normal-state trends of the cuprates, with no separate fitting of each phenomenon.
why: A solution would enable predictive design of high-temperature superconductors rather than empirical search.
key_works: Keimer et al., 2014/2015, *High Temperature Superconductivity in the Cuprates*, arXiv:1409.4673.

title: Cuprate pseudogap identity
open: Which microscopic mechanism — competing order, fractionalization, or a crossover phenomenon — gives rise to the pseudogap in the cuprates, and how does that mechanism connect to superconductivity across different materials and doping levels?
status: Spectroscopy establishes a robust phenomenology, but a single agreed microscopic interpretation is lacking. Key works include Keimer et al., 2014/2015, arXiv:1409.4673, and Timusk and Statt, 1999, *The Pseudogap in High-Temperature Superconductors: An Experimental Survey*.
solved_when: A single microscopic interpretation of the pseudogap is identified that is consistent with the established spectroscopic phenomenology and explains its relation to superconductivity across materials and doping.
why: It resolves a major organizing feature of correlated-electron phase diagrams.
key_works: Keimer et al., 2014/2015, arXiv:1409.4673; Timusk and Statt, 1999, *The Pseudogap in High-Temperature Superconductors: An Experimental Survey*.

title: Superconducting phases of UTe2
open: What order parameters characterize the multiple superconducting phases of UTe2 as field and pressure are tuned, and how do the transitions between them unfold? More precisely, can the pairing symmetries of each field- and pressure-dependent superconducting phase be identified and assigned?
status: Since its 2019 discovery, experiments have revealed an unusually rich phase diagram, but assigning each phase a microscopic order parameter remains contested. Key works include Ran et al., 2019, *Nearly Ferromagnetic Spin-Triplet Superconductivity*, and Hayes et al., 2020, *Weyl Superconductivity in UTe2*, arXiv:2002.02539.
solved_when: Each superconducting phase of UTe2 in the field- and pressure-dependent phase diagram has an assigned microscopic pairing symmetry, with the phase transitions among them accounted for consistently.
why: A solution would test spin-triplet and topological superconductivity in a strongly correlated material.
key_works: Ran et al., 2019, *Nearly Ferromagnetic Spin-Triplet Superconductivity*; Hayes et al., 2020, *Weyl Superconductivity in UTe2*, arXiv:2002.02539.

title: Pairing mechanism in nickelate superconductors
open: What binds electrons into Cooper pairs in the nickelate superconductors? A satisfactory answer must identify the low-energy orbitals involved, the pairing symmetry, and the underlying interaction mechanism, consistently across nickelate families and pressure regimes.
status: Superconductivity was established in nickelates (Li et al., 2019, *Superconductivity in an Infinite-Layer Nickelate*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1496-5), creating a new comparison with cuprates, with signatures of superconductivity near 80 K later found in a nickelate under high pressure (Sun et al., 2023, *Signatures of Superconductivity near 80 K in a Nickelate under High Pressure*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06408-7); however, different structures and dimensionalities complicate a unified interpretation.
solved_when: A single, experimentally verified account specifies the relevant low-energy orbitals, the pairing symmetry, and the interaction mechanism, and applies uniformly across the known nickelate families and pressure regimes (including the infinite-layer materials and the high-pressure regime where superconductivity appears near 80 K).
why: It tests how transferable proposed high-temperature pairing mechanisms really are, using nickelates as a controlled comparison to the cuprates.
key_works: Li et al., 2019, *Superconductivity in an Infinite-Layer Nickelate*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1496-5; Sun et al., 2023, *Signatures of Superconductivity near 80 K in a Nickelate under High Pressure*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06408-7.

title: Topological order of the ν=5/2 fractional quantum Hall state
open: What topological order does the ν=5/2 fractional quantum Hall state actually realize? A determination should specify the realized order, edge structure, and quasiparticle statistics across controlled sample conditions, distinguishing among the competing paired states.
status: Interferometry and thermal transport provide important constraints, but disorder and edge equilibration complicate interpretation. Key works: Moore and Read, 1991, *Nonabelions in the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect*; Banerjee et al., 2018, *Observation of Half-Integer Thermal Hall Conductance*.
solved_when: The realized topological order, edge structure, and quasiparticle statistics of the ν=5/2 state have been determined across controlled sample conditions in a way that discriminates among the competing paired states.
why: It identifies a prominent candidate platform for non-Abelian anyons.
key_works: Moore and Read, 1991, *Nonabelions in the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect*; Banerjee et al., 2018, *Observation of Half-Integer Thermal Hall Conductance*.

title: Reliable low-energy skyrmion transport
open: Can magnetic skyrmions be moved, created, and read reproducibly at low energy, while suppressing pinning, annihilation, thermal errors, and unwanted transverse motion? Formally stated, the goal is a device operating regime in which all of these error and dissipation channels are simultaneously controlled.
status: Individual effects and devices have been demonstrated, but a manufacturable, reliable operating envelope remains an open systems problem. Key works: Fert, Reyren, and Cros, 2017, *Magnetic Skyrmions: Advances in Physics and Potential Applications*; Nagaosa and Tokura, 2013, *Topological Properties and Dynamics of Magnetic Skyrmions*.
solved_when: A manufacturable, reliable operating envelope exists in which skyrmion motion, creation, and readout are reproducible at low energy, with pinning, annihilation, thermal errors, and unwanted transverse motion all suppressed as part of a working system.
why: It would unlock practical topological magnetic memory and logic.
key_works: Fert, Reyren, and Cros, 2017, *Magnetic Skyrmions: Advances in Physics and Potential Applications*; Nagaosa and Tokura, 2013, *Topological Properties and Dynamics of Magnetic Skyrmions*.

title: Existence of an ideal glass transition
subfield: Statistical mechanics and nonequilibrium quantum matter
open: Do glass-forming systems in finite dimensions undergo a genuine thermodynamic ideal-glass transition, or do they merely exhibit dynamics that slow down indefinitely without any true phase change?
status: Competing theories explain important phenomenology, but experimental equilibration becomes inaccessible before the proposed transition in many systems. Key works: Berthier and Biroli, 2011, *Theoretical Perspective on the Glass Transition and Amorphous Materials*, arXiv:1011.2578.
solved_when: A rigorous demonstration, for specified finite-dimensional glass-forming systems, that either a thermodynamic ideal-glass transition exists or that the observed behavior arises from increasingly slow dynamics alone.
why: It determines whether glass formation is fundamentally thermodynamic, dynamical, or both.
key_works: Berthier and Biroli, 2011, *Theoretical Perspective on the Glass Transition and Amorphous Materials*, arXiv:1011.2578.

title: Eigenstate thermalization from microscopic assumptions
subfield: Statistical mechanics and nonequilibrium quantum matter
open: Can eigenstate thermalization be derived as a theorem for broad classes of nonintegrable local Hamiltonians, starting from microscopic assumptions on the dynamics rather than postulating random-matrix behavior? A satisfactory answer should identify which hypotheses are needed and which Hamiltonians fall outside them.
status: The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis has extensive numerical support and many special results, but no universal theorem exists for generic physical Hamiltonians. Key works include Deutsch, 1991, *Quantum Statistical Mechanics in a Closed System*; and Srednicki, 1994, *Chaos and Quantum Thermalization*, cond-mat/9403051.
solved_when: A derivation of eigenstate-thermalization behavior is established for generic nonintegrable local Hamiltonians from stated microscopic assumptions, with the assumptions and exceptions explicitly characterized, so that random-matrix postulates are no longer required.
why: It would ground statistical mechanics directly in the dynamics of closed quantum systems, explaining why thermal behavior emerges without external baths.
key_works: Deutsch, 1991, *Quantum Statistical Mechanics in a Closed System*; Srednicki, 1994, *Chaos and Quantum Thermalization*, cond-mat/9403051.

title: Entropy production from partially observed trajectories
subfield: Statistical mechanics and nonequilibrium quantum matter
open: How much entropy is a system really producing when we can only watch part of it? The goal is to infer tight, experimentally useful bounds on total entropy production from partially observed trajectories, allowing the underlying dynamics to be non-Markovian.
status: Fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic uncertainty relations solve important idealized cases; hidden dissipation remains difficult to reconstruct. Key background: Udo Seifert, 2012, *Stochastic Thermodynamics, Fluctuation Theorems, and Molecular Machines*, arXiv:1205.4176.
solved_when: A method exists that, given trajectories of only a subset of variables of a possibly non-Markovian system, yields bounds on total entropy production that are tight and experimentally usable.
why: It would make nonequilibrium thermodynamics operational in cells and nanoscale devices, where full-state observation is impossible.
key_works: Udo Seifert, 2012, *Stochastic Thermodynamics, Fluctuation Theorems, and Molecular Machines*, arXiv:1205.4176.

title: Universal description of frictional jamming
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Can we build a universal theoretical description of frictional granular jamming, predicting jamming thresholds and mechanical response as functions of friction, particle shape, preparation history, and contact-network evolution?
status: Frictionless spherical-particle jamming is much better organized theoretically than realistic frictional grains; see Liu and Nagel, 2010, *The Jamming Transition and the Marginally Jammed Solid*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-070909-104045.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that yields jamming thresholds and mechanical response as functions of friction, particle shape, preparation history, and contact-network evolution, matching the level of theoretical organization achieved for the frictionless spherical-particle case.
why: It would enable reliable modeling of powders, soils, and dense suspensions, and predictive constitutive laws for history-dependent granular media of interest in civil engineering.
key_works: Liu and Nagel, 2010, *The Jamming Transition and the Marginally Jammed Solid*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-070909-104045.

title: Yielding universality in amorphous solids
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Do all yielding transitions in amorphous solids fall into a single universality class, or does the critical behavior depend on how the material was prepared, aged, its temperature, or the range of its interactions? Formally, determine which yielding transitions share universal critical behavior and which depend on preparation, aging, temperature, or interaction range.
status: Elastoplastic models and simulations reveal avalanche scaling, but brittle yielding, ductile flow, and finite-temperature behavior are not unified. Key works: Bonn et al., 2017, *Yield Stress Materials in Soft Condensed Matter*, arXiv:1502.05281; DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.035005.
solved_when: A unified framework (or a sharp classification) is established that either exhibits a common set of avalanche critical exponents across yielding transitions or identifies which exponents and scaling functions vary with preparation, aging, temperature, or interaction range, covering brittle yielding, ductile flow, and finite-temperature behavior.
why: It provides predictive power over failure and flow in glasses, pastes, and other amorphous materials, where the onset of yielding governs whether a material fractures or flows.
key_works: Bonn et al., 2017, *Yield Stress Materials in Soft Condensed Matter*, arXiv:1502.05281; DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.035005.

title: Predictive discontinuous shear thickening
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Can we predict from first principles when a real dense suspension will abruptly thicken under shear? A successful theory should capture contact activation together with particle roughness, boundary effects, and transient loading in real materials.
status: Frictional-contact models explain much of the phenomenon, notably Wyart and Cates, 2014, *Discontinuous Shear Thickening without Inertia in Dense Non-Brownian Suspensions*, arXiv:1311.4099, but quantitative transfer across particle chemistries and industrial formulations remains incomplete.
solved_when: A quantitative predictive framework exists that forecasts the onset of discontinuous shear thickening in real suspensions, accounting for contact activation, particle roughness, boundary effects, and transient loading, and transfers quantitatively across particle chemistries and industrial formulations.
why: It would enable better processing of concentrated suspensions and the design of impact-responsive materials.
key_works: Wyart and Cates, 2014, *Discontinuous Shear Thickening without Inertia in Dense Non-Brownian Suspensions*, arXiv:1311.4099.

title: Motility-induced phase separation with realistic interactions
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: When does motility-induced phase separation survive in realistic active suspensions — that is, once hydrodynamics, alignment, inertia, chemical signaling, and particle asymmetry are present? A satisfying answer would characterize the conditions under which the phase separation seen in minimal models persists, or is qualitatively altered, under these experimentally relevant interactions.
status: Minimal models exhibit clear phase separation, but adding real-world interactions can qualitatively alter it. Key work: Cates and Tailleur, 2015, *Motility-Induced Phase Separation*, arXiv:1406.3533.
solved_when: A theoretical criterion is established determining for which combinations of hydrodynamics, alignment, inertia, chemical signaling, and particle asymmetry motility-induced phase separation persists, and this criterion correctly predicts the behavior of experimentally realistic active suspensions.
why: It would turn an idealized active-matter mechanism into a predictive material principle for designing and controlling real active suspensions.
key_works: Cates and Tailleur, 2015, *Motility-Induced Phase Separation*, arXiv:1406.3533.

title: Statistical theory of active turbulence
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Can we build a predictive statistical theory of active turbulence — the chaotic, self-driven flow states of active matter — covering how defects are created and annihilated, and how flow spectra and energy transfer behave across different geometries and activity levels? More formally, the goal is to derive universal statistics and defect–flow closures for active turbulent phases from the underlying continuum dynamics.
status: Continuum theories reproduce the characteristic chaotic flows of active turbulence, but universal scaling laws and defect–flow closures remain incomplete. Key work: Marchetti et al., 2013, *Hydrodynamics of Soft Active Matter*, arXiv:1207.2929.
solved_when: A theory exists that quantitatively predicts defect creation and annihilation statistics, flow spectra, and energy transfer in active turbulent phases, and remains valid across varying geometry and activity.
why: Such a theory would enable control of self-driven materials and biological flows, from synthetic active fluids to living-matter systems.
key_works: Marchetti et al., 2013, *Hydrodynamics of Soft Active Matter*, arXiv:1207.2929.

title: Predictive moving-contact-line law
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Can we predict how fast a liquid contact line will move across a real, chemically and physically heterogeneous surface? The goal is a transferable law connecting molecular slip, hysteresis, evaporation, and macroscopic fluid motion on such realistic substrates.
status: The classical no-slip singularity is understood, and many regularizations have been proposed, but choosing among them and parameterizing them predictively remains difficult. Key works: Huh and Scriven, 1971, *Hydrodynamic Model of Steady Movement of a Solid/Liquid/Fluid Contact Line*; Snoeijer and Andreotti, 2013, *Moving Contact Lines: Scales, Regimes, and Dynamical Transitions*.
solved_when: A derived, transferable law exists for contact-line motion on realistic heterogeneous surfaces that quantitatively connects molecular slip, hysteresis, evaporation, and macroscopic fluid motion, and whose parameters can be chosen predictively rather than fitted case by case.
why: A predictive law would directly improve coating, printing, condensation, and microfluidic processes, where contact-line dynamics currently limit control.
key_works: Huh and Scriven, 1971, *Hydrodynamic Model of Steady Movement of a Solid/Liquid/Fluid Contact Line*; Snoeijer and Andreotti, 2013, *Moving Contact Lines: Scales, Regimes, and Dynamical Transitions*.

title: Polymer entanglement under strong deformation
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Can the stress response, disentanglement, and recovery of real polymer melts under strong, complex flows be predicted from molecular architecture alone? In other words, can a first-principles theory replace extensive empirical closure relations?
status: Tube and reptation models capture many regimes; branching, constraint release, nonlinear flow, and failure require additional modeling. Key works: de Gennes, 1971, *Reptation of a Polymer Chain in the Presence of Fixed Obstacles*; Doi and Edwards, 1986, *The Theory of Polymer Dynamics*.
solved_when: A predictive theory derives stress, disentanglement, and recovery under strong, complex deformation directly from molecular architecture, without extensive empirical closure.
why: It would enable predictable manufacturing and recycling of polymeric materials.
key_works: de Gennes, 1971, *Reptation of a Polymer Chain in the Presence of Fixed Obstacles*; Doi and Edwards, 1986, *The Theory of Polymer Dynamics*.

title: Asymptotic wall-turbulence law
open: What is the correct high-Reynolds-number scaling law for wall turbulence? In particular, determine the logarithmic-law coefficients, the nature of outer-layer interactions with the near-wall region, and the limits of any universality.
status: Experiments and simulations span growing ranges of Reynolds number but remain far from many engineering and geophysical regimes. Key works: Marusic et al., 2010, *Wall-Bounded Turbulent Flows at High Reynolds Numbers: Recent Advances and Key Issues*; Smits, McKeon, and Marusic, 2011, *High-Reynolds Number Wall Turbulence*.
solved_when: A validated asymptotic account of wall turbulence at high Reynolds number is established, specifying the logarithmic-law coefficients, characterizing outer-layer interactions, and delimiting universality — consistent with the available experimental and simulation data.
why: It would improve prediction of drag and heat transfer at realistic engineering and geophysical scales, where current data cannot reach directly.
key_works: Marusic et al., 2010, *Wall-Bounded Turbulent Flows at High Reynolds Numbers: Recent Advances and Key Issues*; Smits, McKeon, and Marusic, 2011, *High-Reynolds Number Wall Turbulence*.

title: Three-dimensional turbulent separation prediction
open: Can we predict where separation begins, where the flow reattaches, and what unsteady loads arise in three-dimensional turbulent boundary layers — without tuning the model to each specific geometry?
status: Reynolds-averaged models remain unreliable in many strongly separated flows, while high-fidelity simulation is often too expensive; machine learning approaches face the challenge of generalizing turbulence closures outside their training geometries. Key works include Simpson, 1989, *Turbulent Boundary-Layer Separation*, and Spalart, 2009, *Detached-Eddy Simulation*.
solved_when: A predictive capability exists for separation onset, reattachment location, and unsteady loads in three-dimensional turbulent boundary layers that requires no geometry-specific tuning.
why: It would reduce design uncertainty in vehicles, turbines, and aerodynamic systems, replacing expensive trial-and-error with trustworthy prediction.
key_works: Simpson, 1989, *Turbulent Boundary-Layer Separation*; Spalart, 2009, *Detached-Eddy Simulation*.

title: Turbulent entrainment closure
open: Can we predict the rate at which turbulence entrains irrotulent fluid across turbulent/non-turbulent interfaces in jets, plumes, wakes, and stratified flows from local interfacial physics and large-scale constraints alone, without fitting to each flow class?
status: No predictive closure exists; empirical entrainment coefficients perform adequately within a given flow class but vary with buoyancy, geometry, and intermittency. Key works: da Silva et al., 2014, *Interfacial Layers between Regions of Different Turbulence Intensity*; Frisch, 1995, *Turbulence*.
solved_when: A closure derived from first principles reproduces measured entrainment rates across jets, plumes, wakes, and stratified flows, capturing the observed dependence on buoyancy, geometry, and intermittency.
why: It would replace class-by-class empirical coefficients in models of pollution dispersal, fires, clouds, and industrial mixing with predictive physics.
key_works: da Silva et al., 2014, *Interfacial Layers between Regions of Different Turbulence Intensity*; Frisch, 1995, *Turbulence*.

title: Roughness-to-drag prediction
open: Can drag and heat transfer be predicted directly from measured three-dimensional surface topography, across roughness shapes and Reynolds numbers, without calibrating a model separately for each surface? In other words, is there a physically sufficient descriptor of arbitrary roughness that maps to hydrodynamic outcome without surface-specific tuning?
status: Equivalent-sand-grain descriptions compress observations but do not uniquely follow from arbitrary topography. Key works: Flack and Schultz, 2010, *Review of Hydraulic Roughness Scales in the Fully Rough Regime*; Jiménez, 2004, *Turbulent Flows over Rough Walls*.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that takes measured 3D topography as input and yields drag and heat-transfer predictions valid across roughness shapes and Reynolds numbers, with no dedicated calibration for each surface.
why: It would enable rational design and maintenance of ships, pipes, and turbines rather than case-by-case empirical calibration.
key_works: Flack and Schultz, 2010, *Review of Hydraulic Roughness Scales in the Fully Rough Regime*; Jiménez, 2004, *Turbulent Flows over Rough Walls*.

title: Classical-to-quantum turbulent cascade crossover
open: How does energy injected into a superfluid at large scales cascade down through quantized vortex dynamics into Kelvin waves and ultimately into dissipative excitations, and can this cascade be described by quantitatively testable spectra?
status: Different temperature regimes and vortex configurations support competing crossover pictures; no consensus cascade description exists yet. See Barenghi, Skrbek, and Sreenivasan, 2014, *Introduction to Quantum Turbulence*, arXiv:1404.1909.
solved_when: A theoretical account of the energy transfer route from large-scale superfluid flow through vortex reconnection and Kelvin-wave excitation to dissipation is given, together with predicted spectra that are quantitatively testable against experiment.
why: It would tie classical turbulence phenomenology to the dynamics of quantized topological defects, showing how familiar cascade physics emerges from — or is modified by — quantum constraints on vorticity.
key_works: Barenghi, Skrbek, and Sreenivasan, 2014, *Introduction to Quantum Turbulence*, arXiv:1404.1909.

title: Closed tritium fuel cycle
open: Can a deuterium–tritium fusion plant run its own fuel cycle, producing at least as much tritium as it burns and recovering it fast enough to keep the machine supplied? The open problem is to demonstrate, in an integrated system, a fuel cycle with adequate breeding margin, extraction, inventory control, processing speed, and startup supply.
status: Component tests and blanket designs exist, but neutron economy alone does not establish plant-level self-sufficiency. The problem is highlighted in National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.
solved_when: An integrated deuterium–tritium fuel cycle is demonstrated with adequate breeding margin, extraction, inventory control, processing speed, and startup supply — i.e., plant-level tritium self-sufficiency is achieved rather than inferred from neutron economy alone.
why: It determines whether deuterium–tritium fusion can expand beyond limited external fuel supplies.
key_works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Reactor-compatible divertor exhaust
open: Can a divertor exhaust system simultaneously handle reactor-level heat and particle fluxes while preserving core confinement? Formally, the problem is to find an exhaust configuration and operating regime that controls impurities and keeps target erosion and component temperatures within acceptable limits without degrading the core plasma.
status: Detached plasmas and advanced geometries offer partial solutions, but integrated compatibility of exhaust with core performance remains the key unsolved constraint. Key works: Leonard, 2018, *Plasma Detachment in Divertor Tokamaks*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.
solved_when: A divertor solution is demonstrated that exhausts reactor-level heat and particle fluxes while preserving core confinement, controlling impurities, and maintaining target erosion and component temperatures at acceptable levels.
why: It prevents plasma-facing components from becoming the limiting reactor subsystem, which would otherwise cap the performance of an otherwise viable fusion reactor.
key_works: Leonard, 2018, *Plasma Detachment in Divertor Tokamaks*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Fusion-neutron material lifetime
open: Can structural and functional materials be developed that retain acceptable toughness, dimensional stability, activation, and property retention under relevant fusion-neutron spectra and accumulated damage?
status: Fission irradiation and ion beams provide partial surrogates, but helium production and coupled damage complicate extrapolation to fusion conditions. Key works: Zinkle and Ghoniem, 2000, *Operating Temperature Windows for Fusion Reactor Structural Materials*; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.
solved_when: A material is demonstrated — under neutron spectra and accumulated damage levels relevant to fusion — that meets acceptable targets for toughness, dimensional stability, activation, and property retention.
why: This determines replacement schedules, waste characteristics, and plant economics of fusion power plants.
key_works: Zinkle and Ghoniem, 2000, *Operating Temperature Windows for Fusion Reactor Structural Materials*; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Repetitive, efficient inertial-fusion driver and target system
open: Can an inertial-fusion driver and target system be built that fires repetitively, efficiently, and economically as a whole? Formally, can sufficiently efficient drivers, inexpensive targets, high repetition rate, accurate target injection, and chamber clearing be integrated into a sustained inertial-fusion energy system?
status: Ignition experiments demonstrate target physics, but they do not by themselves establish repetitive economic operation. Key context: National Research Council, 2013, *An Assessment of the Prospects for Inertial Fusion Energy*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*. A related challenge is high-throughput production of precision cryogenic targets.
solved_when: A sustained, integrated inertial-fusion energy system is demonstrated that combines sufficiently efficient drivers, inexpensive targets, high repetition-rate operation, accurate target injection, and chamber clearing — beyond single-shot ignition.
why: It converts individual high-gain shots into a possible power plant; ignition alone does not establish repetitive economic operation.
key_works: National Research Council, 2013, *An Assessment of the Prospects for Inertial Fusion Energy*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Reconnection energy partition
open: How does three-dimensional magnetic reconnection divide its released energy among bulk flow, electron heating, ion heating, and nonthermal particles? A satisfactory answer would take the form of a transferable prediction, valid across plasma regimes, of this energy partition.
status: Kinetic simulations and spacecraft observations establish multiple energy-conversion mechanisms, but a transferable closure predicting the partition remains incomplete. Key works: Zweibel and Yamada, 2009, *Magnetic Reconnection in Astrophysical and Laboratory Plasmas*; Califano et al., 2020, *Electron-Only Reconnection in Plasma Turbulence*, DOI: 10.3389/fphy.2020.00317.
solved_when: A quantitative, regime-dependent framework predicts the partition of released energy among bulk flow, electron heating, ion heating, and nonthermal particles in three-dimensional reconnection, consistent with kinetic simulations and spacecraft observations.
why: It connects magnetic topology changes to observable heating and acceleration, letting observations of energized plasmas be read as signatures of the underlying reconnection process.
key_works: Zweibel and Yamada, 2009, *Magnetic Reconnection in Astrophysical and Laboratory Plasmas*; Califano et al., 2020, *Electron-Only Reconnection in Plasma Turbulence*, DOI: 10.3389/fphy.2020.00317.

title: Predictive low-temperature plasma chemistry
open: Can nonequilibrium, low-temperature plasmas of technological interest be predicted from first inputs — that is, can species concentrations, surface reactions, and energy efficiency be computed a priori from validated cross sections and reaction networks rather than fitted to each device?
status: Current models often depend on incomplete rate data and poorly known surface conditions, and their transfer between reactors is limited. See Adamovich et al., 2022, *The 2022 Plasma Roadmap: Low Temperature Plasma Science and Technology*, DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/ac5e1c.
solved_when: A model built on validated cross sections and reaction networks reproduces species concentrations, surface reaction outcomes, and energy efficiency in a technologically relevant nonequilibrium plasma, and its predictions transfer between reactors without refitting.
why: Reliable prediction would sharpen semiconductor processing, plasma chemical conversion, and plasma-enabled treatment, replacing device-by-device empirical tuning with transferable models.
key_works: Adamovich et al., 2022, *The 2022 Plasma Roadmap: Low Temperature Plasma Science and Technology*, DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/ac5e1c.

title: Nonperturbative strong-field QED regime
open: Can laboratory experiments reach and diagnose the regime where higher-order strong-field quantum corrections qualitatively alter predictions, with beams and fields characterized well enough to distinguish those corrections?
status: Existing experiments constrain radiation reaction and strong-field processes, but accessing the most extreme quantum regime remains a distinct target. Yakimenko et al., 2019, *Prospect of Studying Nonperturbative QED with Beam–Beam Collisions*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.190404.
solved_when: An experiment enters the nonperturbative strong-field quantum electrodynamics regime and demonstrates, with controlled beam and field characterization, that predictions are qualitatively changed by higher-order quantum corrections rather than lower-order descriptions alone.
why: It would test directly where commonly used perturbative descriptions of strong-field QED break down, marking the first controlled observation of that breakdown.
key_works: Yakimenko et al., 2019, *Prospect of Studying Nonperturbative QED with Beam–Beam Collisions*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.190404.

title: Quantum-coherent microwave–optical transduction
open: Can quantum states be converted between microwave and optical frequencies with simultaneously high efficiency, low added noise, adequate bandwidth, and compatible cryogenic operation? Formally, this asks for a transducer that achieves all of these metrics together rather than trading one against another.
status: Multiple physical platforms demonstrate conversion, but optimizing one metric often worsens another. Key works include Lauk et al., 2020, *Perspectives on Quantum Transduction*; Han et al., 2021, *Microwave–Optical Quantum Frequency Conversion*; and Caleffi et al., 2025, *Quantum Transduction: Enabling Quantum Networking*, arXiv:2505.02057.
solved_when: A transduction scheme demonstrates high efficiency, low added noise, adequate bandwidth, and compatible cryogenic operation simultaneously, rather than optimizing one metric at the expense of another.
why: It would connect superconducting quantum processors to optical networks, enabling quantum networking of microwave-based quantum computers.
key_works: Lauk et al., 2020, *Perspectives on Quantum Transduction*; Han et al., 2021, *Microwave–Optical Quantum Frequency Conversion*; Caleffi et al., 2025, *Quantum Transduction: Enabling Quantum Networking*, arXiv:2505.02057.

title: Deterministic low-loss photonic entangling gate
open: Can we build a deterministic two-photon entangling gate whose loss and error rates are low enough for fault tolerance, integrated with the necessary sources, mode matching, and feed-forward? In other words, can such a gate be implemented scalably, rather than only in proof-of-principle demonstrations?
status: Both linear-optical and matter-mediated approaches have achieved important demonstrations, but deterministic high-performance integration remains difficult. Key works include Knill, Laflamme, and Milburn, 2001, *A Scheme for Efficient Quantum Computation with Linear Optics*, and Shapiro, 2006, *Single-Photon Kerr Nonlinearities Do Not Help Quantum Computation*.
solved_when: A scalable deterministic two-photon entangling gate is implemented, with photon sources, mode matching, and feed-forward included, and loss and error rates low enough to support fault tolerance.
why: Such a gate is a prerequisite for practical photonic quantum computation and quantum networking.
key_works: Knill, Laflamme, and Milburn, 2001, *A Scheme for Efficient Quantum Computation with Linear Optics*; Shapiro, 2006, *Single-Photon Kerr Nonlinearities Do Not Help Quantum Computation*.

title: Broadband, efficient, manufacturable metalenses
open: Can a metalens be designed and manufactured that delivers large aperture, high numerical aperture, broadband achromatic operation, polarization tolerance, high efficiency, and acceptable fabrication yield all at once? More precisely, can such a device approach the known dispersion limits while meeting a specified combination of these performance targets?
status: Impressive devices exist, but broadband and large-aperture performance face fundamental and manufacturing tradeoffs, as surveyed in Quevedo-Teruel et al., 2019, *Roadmap on Metasurfaces*, DOI: 10.1088/2040-8986/ab161d, and analyzed in Presutti and Monticone, 2020, *Focusing on Bandwidth: Achromatic Metalens Limits*.
solved_when: A demonstrated metalens meets a specified combination of aperture, numerical aperture, bandwidth, polarization tolerance, efficiency, and fabrication yield, while approaching the known dispersion (bandwidth) limits.
why: It would enable compact optical systems without hidden losses or bandwidth restrictions.
key_works: Quevedo-Teruel et al., 2019, *Roadmap on Metasurfaces*, DOI: 10.1088/2040-8986/ab161d; Presutti and Monticone, 2020, *Focusing on Bandwidth: Achromatic Metalens Limits*.

title: Thermal Casimir-force material-response puzzle
open: How can precision measurements of thermal Casimir forces be reconciled with a physically consistent description of the low-frequency electromagnetic response of real materials and its thermal fluctuations?
status: Predictions using different metallic response prescriptions can disagree with measurements and with thermodynamic expectations in different ways; patch potentials and geometry further complicate the comparison. Key work: Klimchitskaya, Mohideen, and Mostepanenko, 2009, *The Casimir Force between Real Materials: Experiment and Theory*, arXiv:0902.4022.
solved_when: A framework is provided that yields predictions consistent with precision force measurements and with thermodynamic expectations simultaneously, across the response prescriptions under dispute.
why: It would clarify equilibrium fluctuation physics and allow precision force measurements to be interpreted without ambiguity from material-response modeling choices.
key_works: Klimchitskaya, Mohideen, and Mostepanenko, 2009, *The Casimir Force between Real Materials: Experiment and Theory*, arXiv:0902.4022.

title: Attainable limits of near-field radiative heat transfer
open: How much heat can broadband near-field thermal radiation actually carry between real bodies? The question is to determine — and physically approach — practical bounds on broadband near-field heat transfer under realistic material dispersion, nonlocality, finite size, and minimum-gap constraints.
status: Large enhancements beyond far-field radiation have been demonstrated, but idealized bounds are not automatically achievable devices. Key works: Polder and van Hove, 1971, *Theory of Radiative Heat Transfer between Closely Spaced Bodies*; Miller, Johnson, and Rodriguez, 2015, *Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer*.
solved_when: A bound on broadband near-field heat transfer is established that incorporates realistic material dispersion, nonlocality, finite size, and minimum-gap constraints, and a device or construction is shown to approach it.
why: It enables thermal control and energy conversion at nanoscale separations; without attainable bounds, demonstrated enhancements cannot be judged against what is physically reachable.
key_works: Polder and van Hove, 1971, *Theory of Radiative Heat Transfer between Closely Spaced Bodies*; Miller, Johnson, and Rodriguez, 2015, *Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer*.

title: Warm-dense-matter equation of state
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Can we predict — and experimentally verify — the thermodynamic and transport properties of matter in the warm-dense regime, where strong coupling, partial ionization, and quantum degeneracy coexist, with uncertainties that are independently validated?
status: First-principles simulations and dynamic-compression experiments currently constrain selected materials and paths, but broad predictive coverage remains incomplete. Key works: Graziani et al., editors, 2014, *Frontiers and Challenges in Warm Dense Matter*; Wadas et al., 2026, *Shock Compression of Liquid Helium to 360 GPa*, DOI: 10.1103/87r3-tgy1.
solved_when: First-principles predictions of thermodynamic and transport properties are available with validated uncertainty bounds, and dynamic-compression measurements independently confirm them across the warm-dense regime, not merely on selected materials and compression paths.
why: Reliable equations of state in this regime underpin planetary science, high-energy-density experiments, and fusion modeling.
key_works: Graziani et al., editors, 2014, *Frontiers and Challenges in Warm Dense Matter*; Wadas et al., 2026, *Shock Compression of Liquid Helium to 360 GPa*, DOI: 10.1103/87r3-tgy1.

title: Experimental liquid–liquid critical point of water
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Is there a liquid–liquid critical point in real water, and can it be established or excluded by experiment? A definitive answer requires measurements that distinguish genuine liquid behavior from crystallization and from model-dependent inference.
status: Simulations support liquid–liquid transitions in several models, beginning with Poole et al., 1992, *Phase Behaviour of Metastable Water*. The most recent claimed advance — Wang, Berrens, and Donadio, 2026, *Direct Observation of Liquid–Liquid Phase Coexistence in Deeply Supercooled Water Using an Accurate Polarizable Multipole Model*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2526573123 — is a simulation study despite its title, not a direct observation in a macroscopic water experiment.
solved_when: A direct experimental measurement on real (macroscopic) water either demonstrates a liquid–liquid critical point or rules it out, with results that cannot be attributed to ice crystallization or to simulation-model dependence.
why: A liquid–liquid critical point could unify the many anomalies of supercooled water into a single physical picture.
key_works: Poole et al., 1992, *Phase Behaviour of Metastable Water*; Wang, Berrens, and Donadio, 2026, *Direct Observation of Liquid–Liquid Phase Coexistence in Deeply Supercooled Water Using an Accurate Polarizable Multipole Model*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2526573123.

title: Predictive heterogeneous ice nucleation
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Can we predict how fast ice nucleates, and by what pathway, on chemically and structurally realistic surfaces — without fitting parameters separately for each substrate? More formally: is a transferable, quantitatively predictive theory of heterogeneous ice nucleation rates achievable from first-principles or molecular-level inputs alone?
status: Atomistic simulations have revealed the mechanisms of ice nucleation, but rare events, surface disorder, and strong temperature dependence currently impede quantitative transfer to predictive rate prediction. Key works: Sanz et al., 2013, *Homogeneous Ice Nucleation at Moderate Supercooling from Molecular Simulation*; Sosso et al., 2016, *Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations*, arXiv:1603.044 nucleation identifier (verify).
solved_when: Nucleation rates and pathways on chemically and structurally realistic surfaces are predicted quantitatively by a framework that is not refit for each substrate, with accuracy sufficient to capture rare-event kinetics and strong temperature dependence.
why: A solution unlocks reliable models of cloud physics, cryopreservation, and icing control, where nucleation on real, disordered surfaces governs behavior.
key_works: Sanz et al., 2013, *Homogeneous Ice Nucleation at Moderate Supercooling from Molecular Simulation*; Sosso et al., 2016, *Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations*, arXiv:1603.044 nucleation identifier (verify).

title: Controlled nonadiabatic molecular dynamics
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Can we predict coupled electronic–nuclear dynamics through conical intersections and charge-transfer events with reliable error estimates for chemically realistic systems? A complete answer would be an affordable, uniformly reliable method whose approximations carry quantitative error bounds.
status: Surface hopping, Ehrenfest dynamics, and wavepacket methods each have important strengths and limitations; no single affordable method is uniformly reliable. Key works include John Tully, 1990, *Molecular Dynamics with Electronic Transitions*; Subotnik et al., 2016, *Understanding the Surface Hopping View of Electronic Transitions and Decoherence*.
solved_when: A method exists that computes coupled electronic–nuclear dynamics through conical intersections and charge-transfer events for chemically realistic systems, with reliable, quantitative error estimates.
why: It would enable predictive photochemistry, catalysis, and radiation-damage modeling.
key_works: John Tully, 1990, *Molecular Dynamics with Electronic Transitions*; Subotnik et al., 2016, *Understanding the Surface Hopping View of Electronic Transitions and Decoherence*.

title: First-principles electrochemical double layer
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Can we predict from first principles how an electrochemical double layer forms — its interfacial structure, capacitance, and reaction energetics — at a controlled electrode potential for realistic electrolytes? A complete theory must account for thermal fluctuations and specific adsorption at the interface.
status: Continuum and atomistic approaches each capture parts of the physics; constant-potential sampling and long timescales remain challenging. Key works include Schmickler and Santos, 2010, *Interfacial Electrochemistry*, and Schwarz and Sundararaman, 2020, *The Electrochemical Interface in First-Principles Calculations*.
solved_when: A first-principles prediction of interfacial structure, capacitance, and reaction energetics at controlled electrode potential is achieved for realistic electrolytes, including fluctuations and specific adsorption.
why: A reliable first-principles treatment of the double layer would directly improve batteries, electrocatalysis, and electrochemical manufacturing.
key_works: Schmickler and Santos, 2010, *Interfacial Electrochemistry*; Schwarz and Sundararaman, 2020, *The Electrochemical Interface in First-Principles Calculations*.

title: Protein-folding kinetics from sequence
open: Can we predict, from a protein's amino-acid sequence and its environment, how the protein folds in time — the pathways, intermediate populations, and rate constants — rather than just the final folded structure?
status: Accurate structure prediction does not solve folding dynamics; as noted in Outeiral, Nissley, and Deane, 2022, *Current Structure Predictors Are Not Learning the Physics of Protein Folding*. Simulations reach useful regimes but remain limited by timescales and force-field errors. Dill and MacCallum, 2012, *The Protein-Folding Problem, 50 Years On* frames the problem's scope.
solved_when: A theory or computational method takes sequence and environmental conditions as input and predicts folding pathways, intermediate populations, and rate constants, not merely the equilibrium structure.
why: Folding dynamics explain misfolding, kinetic traps, and functional conformational changes, none of which are captured by structure prediction alone.
key_works: Dill and MacCallum, 2012, *The Protein-Folding Problem, 50 Years On*; Outeiral, Nissley, and Deane, 2022, *Current Structure Predictors Are Not Learning the Physics of Protein Folding*.

title: Intrinsically disordered protein ensembles in cells
open: Can we predict the conformational ensembles and interaction kinetics of intrinsically disordered proteins as they actually behave inside living cells? Formally, this asks for condition-dependent ensembles and kinetics in crowded, chemically heterogeneous cellular environments, not dilute in vitro conditions.
status: In vitro measurements and simulations constrain the ensembles, but transferring these results into cells remains difficult. Key works include van der Lee et al., 2014, *Classification of Intrinsically Disordered Regions and Proteins*; and Das and Pappu, 2013, *Conformations of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins Are Influenced by Linear Sequence Distributions of Oppositely Charged Residues*.
solved_when: A predictive theory or method yields conformational ensembles and interaction kinetics of disordered proteins that are validated inside crowded, chemically heterogeneous living environments and correctly capture their dependence on cellular conditions.
why: It would connect protein sequence directly to regulation and disease in cases where a single folded structure is inadequate to explain function.
key_works: van der Lee et al., 2014, *Classification of Intrinsically Disordered Regions and Proteins*; Das and Pappu, 2013, *Conformations of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins Are Influenced by Linear Sequence Distributions of Oppositely Charged Residues*.

title: Causal function of biomolecular condensates
open: When does phase separation itself cause a cellular function, rather than merely accompanying changes in concentration, binding, or molecular organization?
status: Many condensates and mechanisms are characterized; separating phase behavior from correlated biochemical effects remains a major experimental challenge. Key works: Banani et al., 2017, *Biomolecular Condensates: Organizers of Cellular Biochemistry*, DOI: 10.1038/nrm.2017.7; Hyman et al., 2014, *Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Biology*.
solved_when: A direct experimental demonstration separates the causal contribution of phase separation from correlated biochemical effects — e.g., by perturbing condensate formation while controlling concentration, binding, and molecular organization — and shows that the cellular function changes as a result of phase separation alone.
why: Without such causal evidence, condensate-targeting interventions lack mechanistic meaning; with it, they become rationally grounded tools for controlling cellular biochemistry.
key_works: Banani et al., 2017, *Biomolecular Condensates: Organizers of Cellular Biochemistry*, DOI: 10.1038/nrm.2017.7; Hyman et al., 2014, *Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Biology*.

title: Predictive chromosome dynamics
open: Can we predict how chromatin organization evolves in time inside the nucleus and how it responds when specific molecular processes are perturbed? In formal terms, the goal is a predictive theory that couples polymer mechanics, loop extrusion, transcription, and nuclear constraints to yield the time-dependent structure of chromosomes, not just their equilibrium contact maps.
status: Contact maps and polymer models already explain many observed structures, but static agreement with such maps does not uniquely identify the underlying dynamics or causal mechanisms. Key works: Dekker and Mirny, 2016, *The 3D Genome as Moderator of Chromosomal Communication*; Fudenberg et al., 2016, *Formation of Chromosomal Domains by Loop Extrusion*.
solved_when: A theory of chromosome dynamics correctly predicts time-dependent chromatin organization and its response to molecular perturbations, going beyond static structural agreement with contact maps.
why: It would connect genome organization directly to gene regulation and to the mechanical integrity of the nucleus, turning descriptive structural models into causal, predictive ones.
