key_works: Dekker and Mirny, 2016, *The 3D Genome as Moderator of Chromosomal Communication*; Fudenberg et al., 2016, *Formation of Chromosomal Domains by Loop Extrusion*.

title: Tissue jamming and unjamming mechanism
open: What mechanisms determine whether a tissue is jammed or unjammed — and can we predict which factor (cell shape, adhesion, propulsion, division, or extracellular matrix) governs fluidization in a given tissue? Formally, this asks for a predictive theory of jamming and unjamming transitions that holds across different tissues.
status: Vertex and active-matter models reproduce important trends, but universal transfer between experimental systems remains incomplete. Key works: Bi et al., 2015, *A Density-Independent Rigidity Transition in Biological Tissues*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3471; Marchetti et al., 2013, arXiv:1207.2929.
solved_when: A theory correctly identifies when each of cell shape, adhesion, propulsion, division, and extracellular matrix controls tissue fluidization and predicts jamming/unjamming transitions in a way that transfers universally between experimental systems.
why: Such a theory would explain collective cell migration, development, and invasion, including how mechanical regulation drives these processes.
key_works: Bi et al., 2015, *A Density-Independent Rigidity Transition in Biological Tissues*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3471; Marchetti et al., 2013, arXiv:1207.2929.

title: Predictive branching morphogenesis
open: Can the branching architecture of an organ — lung, kidney, gland, or other — be predicted from its local rules of growth, mechanics, signaling, and resource constraints? In other words, is there a theory mapping local interaction parameters to organ-specific branching patterns and to their robustness against perturbation?
status: Current models capture selected branching statistics and geometries, but full parameter-to-form prediction across organs remains unfinished. Key works include Hannezo et al., 2017, *A Unifying Theory of Branching Morphogenesis*; Nerger et al., 2021, *Local Accumulation of Extracellular Matrix Regulates Global…* (full title verify), PMCID: PMC8119325.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that takes as input the local growth, mechanical, signaling, and resource parameters of an organ and outputs its characteristic branching pattern and robustness, validated across organs rather than for selected branching statistics or geometries alone.
why: Such a theory would let developmental biology explain how robust anatomical form arises from local rules, and would give tissue engineering principled control over branching architecture in engineered tissues.
key_works: Hannezo et al., 2017, *A Unifying Theory of Branching Morphogenesis*; Nerger et al., 2021, *Local Accumulation of Extracellular Matrix Regulates Global…* (full title verify), PMCID: PMC8119325.

title: In vivo radical-pair magnetoreception
open: How does a radical-pair chemical reaction inside a living organism actually sense the geomagnetic field and translate it into neural information? The goal is to establish the complete molecular-to-neural chain by which a radical-pair reaction detects geomagnetic fields in an organism, including decisive perturbation tests.
status: Molecular experiments and behavioral effects support aspects of the mechanism; identifying the full in vivo sensor and transduction pathway remains incomplete. Key works: Hore and Mouritsen, 2016, *The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545; Luo et al., 2024, radiofrequency-orientation test, DOI: 10.1098/rsif.2024.0133.
solved_when: The full in vivo sensor and its transduction pathway are identified, connecting the radical-pair reaction through to neural readout, with decisive perturbation experiments confirming each link of the chain.
why: It would establish a concrete quantum mechanism operating in biological sensing, replacing plausibility arguments with a verified pathway.
key_works: Hore and Mouritsen, 2016, *The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545; Luo et al., 2024, radiofrequency-orientation test, DOI: 10.1098/rsif.2024.0133.

title: Earth’s core energy budget and dynamo history
open: Can we determine how much heat and compositional power has been available to drive Earth's geodynamo across geological time? A full answer must reconstruct this energy budget consistently with paleomagnetic, thermal, and material constraints.
status: Core conductivity and inner-core age estimates substantially affect the available power, and competing histories remain possible. Key works: Nimmo, 2015, *Energetics of the Core*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.
solved_when: A self-consistent reconstruction of the core's heat and compositional power through geological time is achieved that satisfies all paleomagnetic, thermal, and material constraints.
why: It explains Earth's long-lived magnetic protection and its thermal evolution.
key_works: Nimmo, 2015, *Energetics of the Core*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.

title: Inner-core nucleation paradox
open: How could Earth's solid inner core first nucleate without requiring implausibly large supercooling? A satisfactory answer would be a mechanism consistent with the core's composition and thermal history that resolves the nucleation paradox.
status: The paradox has been sharpened by atomistic simulations, and two-step and heterogeneous nucleation mechanisms offer candidate resolutions, but no uniquely demonstrated nucleation history exists. Key works: Huguet et al., 2018, *Earth's Inner Core Nucleation Paradox*; Sun et al., 2022, *Two-Step Nucleation of the Earth's Inner Core*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2113059119.
solved_when: A physical mechanism is demonstrated that explains inner-core nucleation without implausibly large supercooling and is consistent with the core's composition and thermal history.
why: The answer fixes the onset time of inner-core growth and hence the inner core's contribution to the geodynamo.
key_works: Huguet et al., 2018, *Earth’s Inner Core Nucleation Paradox*; Sun et al., 2022, *Two-Step Nucleation of the Earth’s Inner Core*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2113059119.

title: Mantle rheology across geological timescales
open: Can we derive from first principles the constitutive laws that govern how Earth's mantle deforms — linking mineral defect physics, grain size, water content, stress, and phase changes to large-scale mantle flow? More formally, the goal is a theory that spans the enormous gap between laboratory creep conditions and geological timescales without uncontrolled extrapolation.
status: Laboratory creep experiments and geophysical inversions currently constrain different regimes, and bridging them by extrapolation remains a major uncertainty. Key works: Karato, 2008, *Deformation of Earth Materials*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.
solved_when: A set of constitutive laws is derived that connects microscopic variables (defects, grain size, water content, stress, phase changes) to mantle flow, validated across the laboratory-to-geological scale gap rather than by extrapolation between separate regimes.
why: It would make quantitative models of mantle convection, post-glacial rebound, and tectonic evolution reliable rather than parameter-dependent; today such models carry a major uncertainty from rheological extrapolation.
key_works: Karato, 2008, *Deformation of Earth Materials*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.

title: Initiation and persistence of plate tectonics
open: Under what physical conditions does a planetary lithosphere develop self-sustaining mobile-plate tectonics rather than falling into a stagnant-lid or episodic regime? More formally, what combination of rheological weakening, volatile content, and thermal state allows subduction-like behavior to initiate and then persist over geologic time?
status: Numerical models demonstrate candidate mechanisms, but Earth's onset history and the roles of water and weakening remain disputed. Key works: Bercovici and Ricard, 2014, *Plate Tectonics, Damage and Inheritance*; Korenaga, 2013, *Initiation and Evolution of Plate Tectonics on Earth: Theories and Observations*.
solved_when: A predictive theoretical criterion exists that specifies the physical conditions (e.g., in terms of water content, damage/weakening mechanisms, and thermal evolution) under which a planetary lithosphere sustains mobile plates, and this criterion is consistent with Earth's onset history and the diversity of planetary tectonic regimes.
why: A solution would explain why Earth maintains plate tectonics while other planets do not, and would underpin our understanding of long-term habitability and planetary diversity.
key_works: Bercovici and Ricard, 2014, *Plate Tectonics, Damage and Inheritance*; Korenaga, 2013, *Initiation and Evolution of Plate Tectonics on Earth: Theories and Observations*.

title: Earthquake nucleation under natural fault conditions
open: Which measurable fault-zone variables govern the transition from slow slip to dynamic rupture in realistic heterogeneous, fluid-bearing faults?
status: Laboratory friction laws and geophysical observations constrain the underlying mechanisms, but natural nucleation zones remain poorly observed. Key works: Dieterich, 1979, *Modeling of Rock Friction: 1. Experimental Results and Constitutive Equations*; Scholz, 2019, *The Mechanics of Earthquakes and Faulting*, third edition.
solved_when: A theory identifies the fault-zone observables that control the slow-slip-to-dynamic-rupture transition in realistic heterogeneous, fluid-bearing faults and predicts that transition in a way testable against laboratory and geophysical data.
why: It would ground earthquake hazard models in physics rather than empirical statistics, improving forecasts of when and where slow slip becomes destructive rupture.
key_works: Dieterich, 1979, *Modeling of Rock Friction: 1. Experimental Results and Constitutive Equations*; Scholz, 2019, *The Mechanics of Earthquakes and Faulting*, third edition.

title: Limits of earthquake predictability
open: Which aspects of earthquake occurrence are predictably encoded in accessible observations, and can we establish calibrated gains over baseline probabilistic forecasts?
status: Reliable deterministic short-term prediction is not established. The open target includes quantitative limits, not a promise that every earthquake has a detectable precursor. Key works: Geller et al., 1997, *Earthquakes Cannot Be Predicted*; Jordan et al., 2011, *Operational Earthquake Forecasting: State of Knowledge and Guidelines for Utilization*.
solved_when: A theory or method is given that quantitatively characterizes which features of earthquake occurrence are predictable from accessible observations, together with a demonstration of calibrated forecast skill exceeding baseline probabilistic forecasts.
why: It separates achievable forecasting improvements from unsupported prediction claims.
key_works: Geller et al., 1997, *Earthquakes Cannot Be Predicted*; Jordan et al., 2011, *Operational Earthquake Forecasting: State of Knowledge and Guidelines for Utilization*.

title: Hydrogen–helium demixing in giant planets
open: Where, in the pressure–temperature–composition space of giant-planet interiors, does a hydrogen–helium mixture separate into distinct phases, and how do the transport properties behave across that boundary? A precise determination of this demixing boundary, and of the transport at and near it, should then be reconciled with observed luminosities and composition profiles of the giant planets.
status: High-pressure calculations and experiments constrain portions of the hydrogen–helium phase diagram, but extrapolation to planetary conditions remains uncertain. Key works include Morales et al., 2009, *Phase Separation in Hydrogen–Helium Mixtures at Mbar Pressures*, and McMahon et al., 2012, *The Properties of Hydrogen and Helium under Extreme Conditions*.
solved_when: The phase-separation boundary under giant-planet conditions is determined, together with the associated transport properties, and shown to be consistent with observed luminosity and composition profiles of the giant planets.
why: It explains helium rain and the thermal evolution of giant planets; without it, models of their cooling histories and internal composition cannot be tied to the underlying phase behavior.
key_works: Morales et al., 2009, *Phase Separation in Hydrogen–Helium Mixtures at Mbar Pressures*; McMahon et al., 2012, *The Properties of Hydrogen and Helium under Extreme Conditions*.

title: Ice-giant dynamo composition and geometry
open: Which interior phases and flow geometries can generate the unusual magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune? More precisely, which combinations of composition and convective-region geometry are consistent with the observed fields while also matching the planets' gravity and thermal constraints?
status: Thin-shell and compositionally stratified dynamo models offer explanations, including Stanley and Bloxham, 2004, *Convective-Region Geometry as the Cause of Uranus' and Neptune's Unusual Magnetic Fields* and Redmer et al., 2011, *The Phase Diagram of Water and the Magnetic Fields of Uranus and Neptune*, but the interior structure remains weakly constrained.
solved_when: A dynamo model is identified whose interior phase composition and flow geometry reproduces the unusual magnetic-field morphologies of Uranus and Neptune and is simultaneously consistent with their gravity and thermal constraints.
why: A solution would tie exotic high-pressure matter — superionic and ionic mixtures — directly to observed planetary magnetic behavior, linking material physics to field geometry.
key_works: Stanley and Bloxham, 2004, *Convective-Region Geometry as the Cause of Uranus’ and Neptune’s Unusual Magnetic Fields*; Redmer et al., 2011, *The Phase Diagram of Water and the Magnetic Fields of Uranus and Neptune*.

title: Low-cloud feedback
open: How much do low clouds thicken, thin, or shift as the climate warms and circulation patterns change? More precisely, can we quantify the response of low clouds to warming and circulation changes, including the interactions among turbulence, entrainment, aerosols, and precipitation?
status: Observational constraints have improved, but cloud feedback remains a major contributor to climate-response uncertainty. Key works: Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*, DOI: 10.1038/ngeo2398.
solved_when: Low-cloud feedback is quantified with sufficient precision to reduce cloud feedback's contribution to climate-response uncertainty — that is, a predictive account of how low clouds respond to warming and circulation changes that captures the coupling among turbulence, entrainment, aerosols, and precipitation.
why: Cloud feedback is a major contributor to uncertainty in projected future warming; quantifying the low-cloud response would substantially narrow that uncertainty.
key_works: Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*, DOI: 10.1038/ngeo2398.

title: Aerosol–cloud effective radiative forcing
open: Can we determine the net climate forcing from aerosol–cloud interactions using observationally constrained causal effects rather than correlations alone?
status: Aerosol properties, cloud adjustments, and meteorological confounding leave substantial uncertainty despite improving satellite and process observations. Key works: Li et al., 2026, *Advancing the Quantification of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions with…* (full title verify), DOI: 10.5194/acp-26-7705-2026; *Remaining Aerosol Forcing Uncertainty after Observational…*, 2026 (authors and full title verify).
solved_when: A quantified estimate of aerosol–cloud effective radiative forcing is obtained whose causal effects are constrained by observations, with confounding from aerosol properties, cloud adjustments, and meteorology explicitly accounted for rather than treated as correlation.
why: It improves attribution of past warming and prediction of climate responses to pollution changes.
key_works: Li et al., 2026, *Advancing the Quantification of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions with…* (full title verify), DOI: 10.5194/acp-26-7705-2026; *Remaining Aerosol Forcing Uncertainty after Observational…*, 2026 (authors and full title verify).

title: Convective self-aggregation and organization
open: When does a field of moist convection spontaneously organize itself into clusters, lines, or larger coherent systems rather than remaining scattered? More precisely, can we predict the onset and character of convective self-aggregation, and quantify its consequences for humidity, rainfall extremes, and radiation?
status: Idealized simulations reveal several feedbacks driving aggregation, but their importance in realistic rotating, heterogeneous atmospheres remains unsettled. Key works include Wing et al., 2017, *Convective Self-Aggregation in Numerical Simulations: A Review*, and Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*.
solved_when: A predictive theory identifies when convection organizes into clusters, lines, or larger systems and quantitatively accounts for the resulting effects on humidity, rainfall extremes, and radiation.
why: A solution would sharpen projections of weather extremes and climate sensitivity, since organized convection redistributes moisture and radiation in ways current models struggle to capture.
key_works: Wing et al., 2017, *Convective Self-Aggregation in Numerical Simulations: A Review*; Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*.

title: Ocean mixing closure
open: Can we predict the amount of irreversible mixing produced by internal waves, shear instabilities, convection, and boundary processes in the ocean from first principles? In particular, can such a closure be formulated without assuming a universal mixing efficiency?
status: Dissipation-based estimates and regional measurements are useful in practice, but mixing efficiency and spatial intermittency vary substantially, undermining the assumption of a universal efficiency. Key works include Osborn, 1980, *Estimates of the Local Rate of Vertical Diffusion from Dissipation Measurements*, and Gregg et al., 2018, *Mixing Efficiency in the Ocean*.
solved_when: A predictive closure exists that yields irreversible mixing rates from internal waves, shear instabilities, convection, and boundary processes without assuming a universal mixing efficiency, and its predictions agree with dissipation-based and regional measurements.
why: Irreversible mixing controls ocean heat uptake, nutrient transport, and the overturning circulation, so a reliable closure directly constrains these in climate and ocean models.
key_works: Osborn, 1980, *Estimates of the Local Rate of Vertical Diffusion from Dissipation Measurements*; Gregg et al., 2018, *Mixing Efficiency in the Ocean*.

title: Atlantic overturning stability threshold
open: How stable is the Atlantic overturning circulation to realistic forcing and freshwater perturbations, and can we foresee its collapse? More precisely, what are its stability boundaries, its recovery behavior once perturbed, and the observable indicators that warn of an approaching tipping point?
status: Models exhibit differing sensitivities and thresholds, and a precise collapse date is not established merely by identifying a statistical warning signal. Key works: Stommel, 1961, *Thermohaline Convection with Two Stable Regimes of Flow*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.
solved_when: A characterization of the stability boundaries of Atlantic overturning under realistic forcing and freshwater perturbations, together with its recovery behavior and identifiable observable warning indicators, is established.
why: It constrains a major source of regional climate risk: without such thresholds and indicators, projections of abrupt North Atlantic circulation change remain unanchored.
key_works: Stommel, 1961, *Thermohaline Convection with Two Stable Regimes of Flow*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.

title: Marine ice-sheet retreat and fracture
open: Can we predict how a marine ice sheet's grounding line retreats and loses buttressing, and when hydrofracture or cliff failure sets in, using constitutive laws that are validated across all relevant scales? Formally, the goal is a unified predictive theory coupling grounding-line dynamics, buttressing loss, hydrofracture, and cliff failure.
status: Different model treatments produce materially different high-end sea-level outcomes, and observational constraints on some failure mechanisms are sparse. Key works: Schoof, 2007, *Ice Sheet Grounding Line Dynamics: Steady States, Stability, and Hysteresis*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists whose constitutive laws are validated across the relevant scales and that yields consistent, observationally constrained grounding-line retreat, buttressing loss, hydrofracture, and cliff-failure outcomes.
why: Different model treatments currently produce materially different high-end sea-level outcomes; a validated theory would reduce uncertainty in long-term sea-level rise projections.
key_works: Schoof, 2007, *Ice Sheet Grounding Line Dynamics: Steady States, Stability, and Hysteresis*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.

title: Gravity-wave drag parameterization
open: Can we predict how unresolved atmospheric gravity waves are generated, propagate, break, and deposit their momentum, so that weather and climate models can represent them from first principles rather than tuning?
status: Existing parameterizations reproduce aspects of the atmospheric circulation but depend on uncertain source spectra and breaking assumptions. Key works include Fritts and Alexander, 2003, *Gravity Wave Dynamics and Effects in the Middle Atmosphere*, and Alexander et al., 2010, *Recent Developments in Gravity-Wave Effects in Climate Models and the Global Distribution of Gravity-Wave Momentum Flux*.
solved_when: A parameterization of gravity-wave generation, propagation, breaking, and momentum deposition demonstrates predictive fidelity across weather and climate models without reliance on uncertain, tuned source spectra and breaking assumptions.
why: A physically grounded treatment of these waves would improve middle-atmosphere circulation and its coupling to weather, a linkage current schemes capture only partially.
key_works: Fritts and Alexander, 2003, *Gravity Wave Dynamics and Effects in the Middle Atmosphere*; Alexander et al., 2010, *Recent Developments in Gravity-Wave Effects in Climate Models and the Global Distribution of Gravity-Wave Momentum Flux*.

title: Attainable broadband sound-absorption limits
open: What is the maximum broadband sound absorption that a passive structure can attain when thickness, bandwidth, angle of incidence, and mass are constrained simultaneously — and can designs approaching that limit be physically realized? Formally, the goal is to characterize the attainable absorption frontier under joint causal and material constraints.
status: Causal bounds and highly effective prototypes exist, but jointly optimal, manufacturable designs remain unresolved for many constraint sets. Key works include Yang et al., 2017, *Optimal Sound-Absorbing Structures*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1093/nsr/nwac246.
solved_when: The optimal absorption limit is determined for specified constraint sets (thickness, bandwidth, angle, mass, passive materials), and manufacturable designs are exhibited that attain or approach those bounds.
why: A solution would enable thinner, lighter, and more effective noise-control structures, replacing heuristic designs with provably optimal ones.
key_works: Yang et al., 2017, *Optimal Sound-Absorbing Structures*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1093/nsr/nwac246.

title: Robust broadband underwater acoustic cloaking
open: Can an underwater acoustic cloak be built that substantially suppresses scattering over a prescribed bandwidth and range of incidence angles while surviving realistic pressure, structural loading, manufacturing errors, and environmental change? Formally, the goal is a construction achieving quantified scattering reduction across the specified band and angular window under such real-world perturbations.
status: Existing cloaking demonstrations commonly trade off among bandwidth, angle, size, and robustness; perfect passive cloaking at all frequencies is not the proposed target. Key works: Cummer and Schurig, 2007, *One Path to Acoustic Cloaking*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*.
solved_when: A demonstrated cloak maintains its scattering reduction over the specified bandwidth and angular range under realistic pressure conditions, structural loading, manufacturing tolerances, and changing environments.
why: It advances wave-control methods and enables practical low-scattering structures for underwater acoustics.
key_works: Cummer and Schurig, 2007, *One Path to Acoustic Cloaking*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*.

title: Low-loss nonreciprocal acoustic devices
open: Can we build acoustic isolators that are genuinely useful — combining low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, high isolation, and stable operation at application-relevant amplitudes in a single device?
status: Nonlinear, time-modulated, and actively biased implementations each break reciprocity under different assumptions; practical tradeoffs remain substantial. Key works: Fleury et al., 2014, *Sound Isolation and Giant Linear Nonreciprocity in a Compact Acoustic Circulator*; Coulais et al., 2017, *Static Non-Reciprocity in Mechanical Metamaterials*.
solved_when: A demonstrated acoustic isolator achieves simultaneously low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, high isolation, and stable operation at application-relevant amplitudes.
why: Such devices protect acoustic systems from reflections and enable directional signal processing.
key_works: Fleury et al., 2014, *Sound Isolation and Giant Linear Nonreciprocity in a Compact Acoustic Circulator*; Coulais et al., 2017, *Static Non-Reciprocity in Mechanical Metamaterials*.

title: Nonlinear topological mechanical-wave protection
open: Which topological protections for wave transport survive when mechanical systems are driven at finite amplitude, with strong disorder, damping, and mode coupling? Formally, determine the extent to which topologically protected transport persists beyond the linearized band-theory regime.
status: Linearized band descriptions are well developed, but nonlinear operation can invalidate their assumptions; key works include Kane and Lubensky, 2014, *Topological Boundary Modes in Isostatic Lattices*, and Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-41679-8.
solved_when: A characterization exists of which topological transport protections persist under finite amplitude, strong disorder, damping, and mode coupling in mechanical systems, replacing the linearized band description with a framework valid in the nonlinear regime.
why: It would make topological waveguiding useful beyond small laboratory signals, where linearized descriptions break down.
key_works: Kane and Lubensky, 2014, *Topological Boundary Modes in Isostatic Lattices*; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-41679-8.

title: Reliable mechanical computation
open: Can a mechanical logic or memory device be made reusable and reliable enough to serve as a genuine computing component, rather than a laboratory demonstration? More precisely, can mechanical logic or memory be operated with quantified error rates, fan-out, reset cost, endurance, and environmental robustness?
status: Mechanical gates and memory elements exist; scaling them into reliable computing systems remains a separate problem. Key works include Florijn, Coulais, and van Hecke, 2014, *Programmable Mechanical Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.175503, and Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*.
solved_when: A reusable mechanical logic or memory element is demonstrated together with measured error rates, fan-out, reset cost, endurance, and environmental robustness.
why: It would enable computation in environments where conventional electronics cannot operate.
key_works: Florijn, Coulais, and van Hecke, 2014, *Programmable Mechanical Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.175503; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*.

title: Predictive fatigue lifetime from microstructure
open: Can we predict how long a structural component will survive fatigue — that is, the full distribution of failure times — starting only from knowledge of its microstructure, defects, and environment? Formally, this asks for a microstructure-derived prediction of failure-time distributions under realistic variable-amplitude loading, including crack evolution.
status: Empirical fatigue curves are useful but transfer poorly across manufacturing routes and loading histories; no predictive first-principles account currently bridges microstructure to lifetime under variable-amplitude loading. Key works: Suresh, 1998, *Fatigue of Materials*, second edition; Ritchie, 1999, *Mechanisms of Fatigue-Crack Propagation in Ductile and Brittle Solids*.
solved_when: A validated theory or model predicts the distribution of failure times from microstructure, defects, and environment under realistic variable-amplitude loading, and the predictions transfer across manufacturing routes and loading histories.
why: It would let engineers certify components against rare fatigue failures directly from material characterization, improving safety while cutting the overdesign currently used as insurance against uncertainty.
key_works: Suresh, 1998, *Fatigue of Materials*, second edition; Ritchie, 1999, *Mechanisms of Fatigue-Crack Propagation in Ductile and Brittle Solids*.

title: Quantitative dynamic fracture branching
open: When does a rapidly propagating crack in a three-dimensional heterogeneous material become unstable, and what quantitative law governs how it branches, roughens, or changes propagation mode?
status: Fracture mechanics describes many regimes, but process-zone physics and three-dimensional instabilities remain difficult to close. Key works: Fineberg and Marder, 1999, *Instability in Dynamic Fracture*; Bouchbinder, Fineberg, and Marder, 2010, *Dynamics of Simple Cracks*. Related mathematics concerns moving-boundary singularities and pattern selection.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that quantitatively determines the onset and evolution of branching, roughening, and mode changes of fast-moving cracks in three-dimensional heterogeneous materials, matching when and how rapidly these instabilities occur.
why: It explains rapid catastrophic failure, connecting crack dynamics across regimes to the underlying process-zone physics.
key_works: Fineberg and Marder, 1999, *Instability in Dynamic Fracture*; Bouchbinder, Fineberg, and Marder, 2010, *Dynamics of Simple Cracks*.

title: Damage-tolerant inverse-designed metamaterials
open: Can we design architected metamaterials whose desired mechanical response survives realistic defects, aging, and repeated loading? More formally, the goal is architectures whose robustness is certified by experimentally validated uncertainty, not only by ideal-cell simulations.
status: Inverse design currently produces remarkable nominal responses, but defect tolerance and lifetime remain less mature. Key works: Bertoldi et al., 2017, *Flexible Mechanical Metamaterials*; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*. A related direction is distributionally robust topology optimization.
solved_when: An inverse-designed architecture demonstrates its target mechanical response in the presence of realistic defects, aging, and repeated loading, with the uncertainty validated by experiment rather than ideal-cell simulation alone.
why: It would move architected materials from laboratory demonstrations into dependable, load-bearing structures.
key_works: Bertoldi et al., 2017, *Flexible Mechanical Metamaterials*; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*.

title: High-efficiency multistage plasma acceleration
open: How can many plasma-acceleration stages be coupled into an integrated accelerator while preserving beam quality at high repetition rate and high wall-plug efficiency? Formally, this asks for a staged plasma accelerator whose cascaded nonlinear stages maintain beam emittance and energy spread under sustained, high-duty operation.
status: High gradients and selected staging demonstrations are established, but collider-quality integrated operation remains unresolved (Geddes, Hogan, Musumeci, and Assmann, 2022, *Report of Snowmass 21 Accelerator Frontier Topical Group 6 on Advanced Accelerators*, arXiv:2208.13279).
solved_when: An integrated multistage plasma accelerator demonstrates preserved beam quality across coupled stages while operating at high repetition rate with high wall-plug efficiency.
why: A solution could shrink the size and cost of accelerators, opening collider-scale and broad-application machines now out of practical reach.
key_works: Geddes, Hogan, Musumeci, and Assmann, 2022, *Report of Snowmass 21 Accelerator Frontier Topical Group 6 on Advanced Accelerators*, arXiv:2208.13279.

title: Collider-quality positron plasma acceleration
open: Can positron beams be accelerated in a plasma wakefield to collider quality — preserving low emittance, small energy spread, and useful charge with high efficiency — rather than merely demonstrating energy gain? Formally, this asks for acceleration of positrons meeting the full emittance, energy-spread, charge, and efficiency requirements of a collider application.
status: Plasma structures that naturally favor electron acceleration do not automatically provide equivalent positron performance. Key works: Corde et al., 2015, *Multi-Gigaelectronvolt Acceleration of Positrons in a Self-Loaded Plasma Wakefield*; Geddes et al., 2022, arXiv:2208.13279.
solved_when: A positron beam is plasma-accelerated while simultaneously achieving the emittance, energy spread, charge, and efficiency targets required for collider operation, not just net energy gain.
why: It determines whether plasma acceleration can underpin future electron–positron colliders, the core machine of high-energy physics.
key_works: Corde et al., 2015, *Multi-Gigaelectronvolt Acceleration of Positrons in a Self-Loaded Plasma Wakefield*; Geddes et al., 2022, arXiv:2208.13279.

title: Affordable high-field accelerator dipoles
open: Can long accelerator dipoles operating at high field be manufactured reproducibly and at a cost that makes full magnet strings economical? Success requires simultaneously acceptable quench protection, field quality, conductor cost, training behavior, and lifetime.
status: Record-setting short models exist, but they do not establish economical production of complete magnet strings. Key works: Bottura et al., 2012, *Advanced Accelerator Magnets for Upgrading the LHC*; International Muon Collider Collaboration, 2024, *Interim Report*, arXiv:2407.12450.
solved_when: Complete magnet strings — not just short models — are produced economically with reproducible high-field performance and acceptable quench protection, field quality, conductor cost, training, and lifetime.
why: These magnets determine the feasible collider energy, footprint, and cost; without economical production, high-energy collider designs cannot be realistically priced or built.
key_works: Bottura et al., 2012, *Advanced Accelerator Magnets for Upgrading the LHC*; International Muon Collider Collaboration, 2024, *Interim Report*, arXiv:2407.12450.

title: Radiation-hard picosecond four-dimensional tracking
open: Can a tracking detector be built that delivers fine spatial resolution together with picosecond-class timing, while remaining low mass, drawing manageable power, handling high rates, and surviving the intended radiation dose?
status: Timing sensors demonstrate important capabilities, but simultaneously meeting all next-generation detector requirements is difficult; see Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.
solved_when: A detector design is demonstrated that simultaneously achieves fine spatial resolution, picosecond-class timing, low mass, manageable power, high-rate operation, and survival of the intended radiation dose.
why: Such a detector separates overlapping collisions and expands sensitivity to rare events.
key_works: Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.

title: Tenfold lower-cost cryogenic detector readout
open: Can the total cost and wall-plug power per usable cryogenic detector readout channel be reduced tenfold relative to a declared reference system, while keeping noise, bandwidth, crosstalk, and reliability unchanged?
status: Multiplexing improves selected metrics, but channel count alone does not demonstrate the complete target. Key works: Irwin and Hilton, 2005, *Transition-Edge Sensors*; Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.
solved_when: A demonstrated readout system achieves a tenfold reduction in both total cost and wall-plug power per usable channel against a declared reference system, with noise, bandwidth, crosstalk, and reliability held fixed.
why: It would make very large quantum-sensor and detector arrays practical by removing cost and power as the limiting constraints on scaling.
key_works: Irwin and Hilton, 2005, *Transition-Edge Sensors*; Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.

title: Executable preservation of experimental analyses
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can a complete experimental analysis be preserved such that an independent authorized researcher can rerun it years after the original computing environment disappears? The goal is to preserve not only the data, but also the calibrations, software, experimental conditions, and the expertise needed to execute the full analysis.
status: DPHEP and experiment-specific programs demonstrate feasibility; coverage and long-term operational support remain uneven. Key works: Basaglia et al., 2023, *Data Preservation in High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2302.03583.
solved_when: A published analysis can be faithfully rerun by such a researcher long after the original environment is gone, with data, calibrations, software, conditions, and expertise all preserved and accessible.
why: Without it, expensive scientific data becomes irreproducible and effectively lost, invalidating future reanalysis and verification of published results.
key_works: Basaglia et al., 2023, *Data Preservation in High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2302.03583.

title: Reusable public likelihoods and nuisance correlations
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can experimental collaborations publish likelihoods, response functions, and nuisance-parameter correlations in a form that lets outsiders validly combine results and reinterpret them without reverse-engineering hidden assumptions from published plots?
status: Important tools and releases exist, but the practice is not universal and some analyses are difficult to release faithfully. Key works: Cranmer et al., 2022, *Publishing Statistical Models: Getting the Most out of Particle Physics Experiments*, arXiv:2109.04981; Basaglia et al., 2023, arXiv:2302.03583.
solved_when: A reusable public likelihood release contains sufficient structured likelihood information, response functions, and nuisance correlations to support valid combinations and reinterpretations without reconstructing hidden assumptions from plots.
why: It extracts additional science from existing analyses without repeating experiments.
key_works: Cranmer et al., 2022, *Publishing Statistical Models: Getting the Most out of Particle Physics Experiments*, arXiv:2109.04981; Basaglia et al., 2023, arXiv:2302.03583.

title: Out-of-distribution benchmark for scientific simulators
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can we build a benchmark that measures whether learned scientific simulators remain physically trustworthy outside their training distribution — specifically testing physical accuracy, conservation, uncertainty calibration, and failure detection when the simulator encounters new geometries, scales, materials, or forcing?
status: Existing datasets benchmark pieces of this problem, but a high score on interpolation is not evidence of reliable physical extrapolation; no unified out-of-distribution benchmark yet exists. See Shanahan et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Computational Frontier CompF03 Topical Group Report: Machine Learning*, arXiv:2209.07559.
solved_when: A publicly available benchmark dataset exists that evaluates learned simulators on physical accuracy, conservation, uncertainty calibration, and failure detection under out-of-distribution conditions (new geometries, scales, materials, or forcing), such that strong interpolation performance cannot be mistaken for reliable extrapolation.
why: It prevents accelerated simulation from silently producing scientifically wrong results, which is the central risk of replacing traditional simulators with learned ones in scientific workflows.
key_works: Shanahan et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Computational Frontier CompF03 Topical Group Report: Machine Learning*, arXiv:2209.07559.

title: Cross-platform low-energy-background benchmark
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can we assemble a calibrated, provenance-rich benchmark of unexplained low-energy events measured across different detector materials and laboratories, carrying shared environmental and analysis metadata?
status: Individual experiments have published valuable studies, but cross-platform comparability remains limited; the goal is harmonization of existing data, not the claim that no data exist. Key works: Boveia et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Dark Matter Complementarity Report*, arXiv:2211.07027; Barbeau et al., 2022, instrumentation report.
solved_when: A cross-platform dataset exists that combines calibrated measurements of unexplained low-energy events from multiple detector materials and laboratories, with full provenance and harmonized environmental and analysis metadata, enabling like-for-like comparison.
why: Such a benchmark is what makes it possible to tell a genuinely new physical signal apart from a shared material or instrumental background common to multiple experiments.
key_works: Boveia et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Dark Matter Complementarity Report*, arXiv:2211.07027; Barbeau et al., 2022, instrumentation report.

title: Sustainable helium access and recovery
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: How can we build procurement and recovery systems that keep helium-dependent research reliably supplied at predictable costs, including for smaller laboratories?
status: The APS–ACS–MRS report (APS, ACS, and MRS, 2016, *Responding to the U.S. Research Community’s Liquid Helium Crisis*) documented serious disruption and proposed collective purchasing and recovery; the remaining open target is durable implementation and equitable coverage, not another diagnosis.
solved_when: Durable collective purchasing and helium recovery systems are implemented with equitable coverage across laboratories, including smaller ones.
why: Prevents cryogenic research programs from being determined by supply shocks rather than scientific merit.
key_works: APS, ACS, and MRS, 2016, *Responding to the U.S. Research Community’s Liquid Helium Crisis*.

title: Stable careers and funding for research software maintenance
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can funding agencies and laboratories be equipped with concrete, evaluable funding structures that sustain long-term maintenance, testing, security, and succession planning for critical physics software, rather than structures that reward only the creation of new code?
status: Community roadmaps, including the HEP Software Foundation's 2017/2019 *A Roadmap for HEP Software and Computing R&D for the 2020s* (arXiv:1712.06982), repeatedly identify maintenance and staffing needs for critical physics software. The gap is institutional implementation with measurable continuity, not a missing programming technique.
solved_when: Such funding structures are created and evaluated in practice, demonstrating measurable continuity in maintenance, testing, security, and succession for critical physics software.
why: It reduces scientific risk arising from abandoned or undermaintained computational infrastructure on which physics results depend.
key_works: HEP Software Foundation, 2017/2019, *A Roadmap for HEP Software and Computing R&D for the 2020s*, arXiv:1712.06982.

title: Fusion-relevant shared irradiation qualification
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Can the fusion community establish shared, accessible, and adequately funded irradiation and post-irradiation facilities that produce material-qualification evidence under reactor-relevant spectra, doses, and temperatures?
status: Surrogate irradiation supplies useful information, but facility access and representative exposure remain infrastructure bottlenecks. Key works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.
solved_when: Shared irradiation and post-irradiation examination facilities exist with open access and sustained funding, and routinely deliver material-qualification data at fusion-relevant spectra, doses, and temperatures.
why: Without it, reactor design rests on unvalidated material-lifetime assumptions; surrogate irradiation gives useful information but cannot substitute for representative exposure.
key_works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Laboratory-data funding across disciplinary boundaries
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: How can funding agencies establish accountable routes for supporting laboratory measurements that serve the needs of a different discipline—for example, atomic, molecular, and plasma data essential to interpreting astronomical observations? In formal terms, the problem is to design an institutional and budgetary mechanism under which reference measurements valued primarily by users outside the funding program's own domain receive stable, assignable support.
status: National Academies assessments have identified gaps when facilities, investigators, and scientific beneficiaries fall under different program responsibilities; see National Academies, 2020, *Progress toward Implementation of the 2013 Decadal Survey for Solar and Space Physics: A Midterm Assessment*, discussion of laboratory-data support.
solved_when: A funding mechanism exists in which laboratory measurements needed by another field are explicitly budgeted and administered, so that gaps identified when facilities, investigators, and scientific beneficiaries fall under different program responsibilities no longer leave such measurements unfunded.
why: It prevents major observing facilities from being limited by comparatively inexpensive missing reference measurements—small data gaps that would otherwise cap the scientific return of large infrastructure investments.
key_works: National Academies, 2020, *Progress toward Implementation of the 2013 Decadal Survey for Solar and Space Physics: A Midterm Assessment*, discussion of laboratory-data support.
